@@138273836 <h> Long before modern environmental science , Indian civilisation treated nature not as a resource to exploit but as a sacred web of life <p> On World Environment Day , the Prime Minister remarked that this day serves to reaffirm the commitment to protecting the environment and furthering sustainable growth . The Prime Minister emphasised that this deep cultural ethos is beautifully reflected in traditional Indian wisdom , reinforced with the following message of environmental stewardship : <p> May the air flow pleasantly and beneficially around us , may the rivers provide life-giving and nourishing water , and may herbs and plants bring health and well-being to all living beings . <p> Ancient India developed one of the most sophisticated and holistic approaches to environmental responsibility in human history . Considerably prior to the emergence of the scientific discipline of modern ecology , Indian civilisations integrated conservation into daily life , governance , philosophy and spirituality . This strong awareness of the environment grew from a perspective that viewed humans as an inseparable part of nature . The Panchamahabhutas , the five great elements of earth , water , fire @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and any disruption of their balance was viewed as both unethical and self-destructive . From Vedic texts and community practices to archaeological evidence from the Indus Valley Civilisation and policies under the Mauryas , ancient India sustained biodiversity , soil fertility , water resources and forests for millennia through a multifaceted system of protection . <p> At the core of ancient Indian environmental ethics lay a deep metaphysical sense of interconnectedness . The Vedas ( c. 1500 -- 500 BCE ) abound with hymns that personify natural forces . Earth ( Prithvi ) was worshipped as Prithvi Mata ( mother earth ) , a nurturing goddess whose body sustained life . The Rigveda 's Bhumisukta ( earth hymn ) celebrates her bounty while urging restraint . Humans are advised to not dig too deeply or exploit her excessively which is an early articulation of sustainable resource use . <p> The concept of Rta ( cosmic order or natural law ) anchored this reverence . Rta governed the harmonious functioning of the universe ; human actions were expected to align with it to avoid chaos ( Anrta ) . <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ unyielding ; its manifestations are many , beautiful , and luminous for the sake of the universe . Through Rta , living beings receive sustained nourishment ; by Rta , the cosmic rays ( cows/lights ) have entered into the eternal order . <p> Rivers such as the Ganga , Yamuna and Saraswati were worshipped as goddesses embodying purity and vitality ; polluting or obstructing them was considered a grave sin . The sun ( Surya ) , wind ( Vayu ) , and fire ( Agni ) likewise received devotional hymns . <p> The Upanishads deepened this into a philosophy of unity , with Brahman ( ultimate reality ) pervading all existence and discouraging anthropocentrism . The Bhagavad Gita reinforced the importance of duty ( Dharma ) and detachment while living in harmony with nature . Jainism and Buddhism further strengthened these ethics : Jainism 's Ahimsa extended to all beings , including microscopic life , promoting vegetarianism and minimalism , while Buddhism emphasised compassion ( Karuna ) and mindfulness . Ayurvedic texts linked health to environmental balance and cautioned against pollution and deforestation . <p> The Rigveda ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ banyan ) tree by the roots ; rather , exterminate all evils and unrighteousness .. <p> Tree planting was a spiritual obligation , and forests ( Tapovana ) were regarded as abodes of deities and sages . Later works built upon these foundations . Kautilya 's Arthashastra classified forests into protected reserves ( Abhayaranya ) , production forests for timber and elephant forests . Dedicated officers ( Vanadhyaksha ) enforced regulations , including fines for illegal logging or hunting . <p> Among the most enduring institutions were sacred groves ( Devrai , Kavu , Oran , or Tapovana ) , patches of virgin forest dedicated to local deities and safeguarded by religious taboos . Estimates suggest approximately 100,000 -- 150,000 sacred groves once existed across India , many of which survive today . These no-take zones prohibited tree felling , hunting and firewood collection , preserving endemic species , maintaining microclimates , protecting watersheds and preventing soil erosion . Community enforcement through rituals and folklore supported and nourished them . Regional variations such as Rajasthan 's orans for fodder and water or Northeast Indian groves for montane biodiversity added richness @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ wildlife exemplify this tradition . <p> Water was revered as Jala or Apah . The Indus Civilisation demonstrated advanced urban planning with covered drains , soak pits , wells , reservoirs , and sophisticated rainwater harvesting at sites like Dholavira . Vedic texts stressed water purity , while later periods saw the construction of tanks ( kulam ) , stepwells ( baoli ) and lakes . The Arthashastra outlined rules for water allocation and penalties for pollution . Traditional systems such as johads and eris replenished groundwater through community governance , by blending engineering prowess with ecological wisdom and often involving temples . <p> Ancient Indian agriculture worked in tandem with seasons , treating the soil as a living being . Vedic farming favoured mixed cropping , crop rotation and organic manures . Texts like Krishi Parashara warned against monocultures and excessive irrigation . Biodiversity was supported through sacred plants , while forests were managed sustainably as mandated by the Arthashastra . Cows and other livestock , vital for milk , dung , and traction , were protected by the tenet of Ahimsa . Integrated crop-livestock systems enhanced soil fertility @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ These practices ensured rich biodiversity , fertile soils and resilient communities . Sacred groves remain living laboratories of exceptional species diversity . Globally , India 's model of culturally rooted conservation stands out for its scale and depth . <p> In conclusion , ancient Indian environmentalism was not an incidental by-product of history , but a deliberate , highly integrated socio-ecological paradigm . It fused philosophical concepts ( Ahimsa , Rta ) , ethics , empirical science ( Vrikshayurveda , Ayurveda ) , governance ( Arthashastra ) and community participation . This wisdom ensured the continuity of one of the world 's oldest civilisations and continues to offer valuable insights for ethical coexistence with the planet today . We must apply ancient Indian wisdom to address the present-day escalating impacts of climate change . The Prime Minister 's call to protect the environment is highly timely and will certainly awaken the ecological consciousness of both Indian citizens and the global community . <p> Views expressed are personal . @@138275555 <h> Mainstreaming Climate Action in Urban India <h> Mainstreaming Climate Action in Urban India <p> The future of India 's climate will be determined by its cities . From heatwaves and floods to water stress , cities across the country are already experiencing the impact of climate events . By 2036 , India 's urban population is set to exceed 600 million ; cities must manage unprecedented population growth while strengthening climate resilience . This brief argues that India 's urban climate challenge has moved beyond pilots , plans , and isolated projects . A decisive shift is underway , from treating climate action as a sectoral or environmental concern to an imperative of urban development and governance . Drawing on national policy frameworks and city-level experiences across mitigation , adaptation , and resilience , this brief examines how Indian cities are beginning to integrate climate risk into land-use planning , infrastructural investment , municipal finance , and institutional systems . It highlights emerging pathways for mainstreaming climate action through risk-informed planning , integrated urban systems , outcome-based governance , and scaled urban climate finance . <h> Introduction <p> While @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are the arena of action . They are the largest consumers of energy and the biggest generators of emissions . Globally , urban areas account for nearly 70 percent of energy use and more than 70 percent of carbon dioxide emissions. 1 Cities are where climate change directly intersects with development through land-use decisions , building regulations , transport systems , water and waste services , and municipal investment choices . <p> Climate adaptation in cities is not only an environmental necessity but an economic and social imperative . For instance , extreme heat reduces labour productivity , floods damage assets and infrastructure , and water stress undermines industrial and household security . These conditions affect vulnerable populations much more , including residents of informal settlements , outdoor workers , women , older adults , and individuals with limited access to public services . <p> At present , India 's climate strategy is shaped by its commitment to several international frameworks on sustainability and resilience . The first of these is the 1987 Brundtland Report , which drew attention to the challenges of urban growth and argued that environmental protection @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ addressed in an integrated manner. 2 This thinking was reinforced at the 1992 United Nations ( UN ) Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro , where Agenda 21 encouraged local governments to prepare sustainability plans in consultation with communities and other stakeholders. 3 These frameworks established the expectation that cities would take responsibility for linking sustainability with development . <p> In 2015 , India became a signatory to the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction ( 2015 -- 2030 ) , which sets out a protocol for integrating disaster risk reduction into national and local development strategies and urban planning. 4 <p> India 's approach is also guided by the UN Sustainable Development Goals ( SDGs ) , which emphasise the need for cities to be inclusive , safe , resilient , and sustainable ( SDG 11 : Sustainable Cities and Communities ) , and for urgent steps to combat climate change and its impacts ( SDG 13 : Climate Action ) . <p> Among international frameworks , the Paris Agreement , adopted in 2015 , to which India is a signatory , is the most important . It calls @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ? Celsius ( C ) , with a target of 1.5 ? C , thereby requiring mitigation and adaptation measures . The agreement has shifted the global climate governance regime from negotiated targets towards nationally determined contributions ( NDCs ) . 5 Notably , the Paris framework recognises that climate outcomes depend on delivery across sectors and levels of government . <p> India 's commitment to these international frameworks was highlighted at the 2025 UN Climate Change Conference in Bel ? m , Brazil , where the Indian delegation noted that adaptation , urban resilience , and disaster risk reduction must be treated as core development investments . <h> India 's Climate Action Framework <p> India 's climate policy framework has recognised the critical role that cities play in shaping climate outcomes . In 2008 , the National Action Plan on Climate Change ( NAPCC ) identified eight core missions for India , of which one addresses urban resilience and sustainability ( National Mission on Sustainable Habitat ) . 6 <p> At the subnational level , State Action Plans on Climate Change have enabled states to tailor national climate goals @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are the Smart Cities Mission , Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban , and AMRUT ( Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation ) , 8 which provide funding and guidelines to enhance infrastructural resilience and boost the circular economy . <p> India 's path to achieving its NDCs and SDGs lies through urban governance. 9 Urban local governments must lead climate action through planning , reforms , infrastructure investment , and service provision . National resilience can not be achieved if municipal budgets , land-use plans , and infrastructural investments remain climate-blind . <p> The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act envisaged urban local bodies ( ULBs ) as the third tier of government , mandating the transfer of functions , functionaries , and funds to enable their effective functioning . However , many Indian cities continue to operate with limited fiscal autonomy and inadequate technical and human resources. 10 Despite these constraints , Indian cities are making concerted efforts to realise national and global commitments through climate plans , sectoral investments , reform measures , and institutional innovations . Many of them , for instance , have prepared climate strategies or equivalents , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ) and Bengaluru ( 2023 ) , and the City Climate Action Plans for Pune , Jamnagar , Junagadh , and Leh. 11 However , only a limited number of municipalities have integrated these plans into their budgets , statutory master plans , and routine decision-making processes. 12 <p> Several cities have also joined global climate coalitions , including C40 Cities , 13 ICLEI -- Local Governments for Sustainability , 14 the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy , 15 and the Resilient Cities Network. 16 Participation in these networks provides access to technical assistance , peer learning , global best practices , and climate-planning tools . <h> Indian Initiatives in Urban Climate Action <p> City action towards climate change is meant to address the interlinked objectives of mitigation , adaptation , and resilience . <h> Climate Mitigation <p> Climate mitigation entails reducing emissions from key urban sectors , such as transportation , energy , buildings , and solid waste . National audits , court judgments , and independent studies regularly report instances of unauthorised construction , encroachment into floodplains and coastal areas , and the resulting intensification of climate-related risks . NITI Aayog 's 2021 report on urban planning capacity in India notes that risks such as urban flooding and environmental stress are often amplified by weak rule enforcement and limited institutional capacity , rather than by climate stressors alone. @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ into master plans and development regulations can therefore be viewed as efforts to address long-standing planning deficits and climate-related risks. 41 <h> Climate-Responsive Buildings and Urban Energy Systems <p> Various studies indicate that energy-efficient buildings can reduce energy consumption by up to 70 percent , cut emissions , and reduce heat stress. 42 City governments thus must uniformly enforce the Energy Conservation Building Code and the Eco-Niwas Samhita across commercial and residential buildings. 43 Cool roof programmes can reduce indoor temperatures and energy use , particularly in heat-prone and informal settlements. 44 Finally , retrofitting older buildings for energy efficiency and renewable energy use will help cities transition to low-carbon energy use . <h> Sustainable Urban Mobility and Air Quality Improvement <p> Sustainable urban mobility is essential for reducing emissions and improving air quality. 45 This means prioritising public transport , improving walking and cycling infrastructure , and transitioning to electric vehicles . Strong public transport systems improve access while reducing congestion and vehicle emissions . Cities can also lower travel demand through mixed land use , higher-density development along transit corridors , and transit-oriented development . <p> Doing this @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , public transport , traffic management , and land use . The Unified Metropolitan Transport Authorities ( UMTAs ) , mandated under the Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission in 2005 and reiterated in the Metro Rail Policy in 2017 , are intended to perform this role . Their responsibilities encompass integrated transport planning , fare integration , multimodal connectivity , and coordinated investment decisions . Yet only a limited number of cities have established functional UMTAs. 46 <p> Urban Water Security and Flood Management Systems <p> Water security in cities requires system upgrades and maintenance of municipal piped water networks ; reduction in non-revenue water supply through leak detection and metering ; measures to recharge groundwater ; and the reuse and recycling of wastewater . Furthermore , periodic desilting and rehabilitation of stormwater drainage systems must be undertaken . Cities must also promote nature-based solutions and focus on blue-green infrastructure , such as bioswales , wetlands , and permeable pavements . The sponge city concept pioneered in China , 47 , 48 for instance , aims to enhance the absorption , storage , and reuse of water , thereby @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in several Chinese cities , as well as in other cities worldwide , indicates the effectiveness of nature-based solutions for urban water management. 49 In India , Delhi , Bhopal , Madurai and Bengaluru have prepared blue-green infrastructure master plans. 50 Ensuring that such plans are integrated into statutory development planning across other Tier I and II cities would be a good step forward . <p> Climate-Smart Urban Waste Management <p> For climate action to be effective , waste management needs to begin at the source . Consistent waste segregation enables material recovery , local treatment of organic waste , and waste reduction before landfilling , ultimately preventing the entry of fresh waste into landfills . <p> Cities also need to remediate legacy dump sites and landfills , as they emit methane and contaminate land and water . One solution is to convert waste streams into energy through biogasification and the production of bio-CNG and other waste-to-energy options . <p> Indore offers a noteworthy example of how these approaches can work together . The city processes segregated organic waste to produce bio-CNG , which is then used to fuel parts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ plastic waste management through a combination of recycling , co-processing , and extended producer responsibility . Integrated waste management systems thus have high potential to move cities towards a circular economy. 51 They can reduce emissions and recover value from waste , providing public health , environmental , and social benefits. 52 <p> Data Systems and Urban Climate Governance <p> Data and governance form the backbone of successful climate action . Initiatives like the Smart Cities Mission and the National Urban Digital Mission have strengthened urban data systems through dashboards , command-and-control centres , and service performance tracking. 53 In addition , the Urban Outcomes Framework , 54 Service Level Benchmarking , 55 and the Integrated Command and Control Centre Maturity Assessment Framework56 have improved standardisation and comparability across cities . But climate-related data is yet to be adequately linked to planning , budgeting , and service delivery . <p> There is also increasing global attention on measuring adaptation . New indicators under the Global Goal on Adaptation reflect a shift towards outcome-based rather than input-based tracking . To achieve this , global indicators need to be customised to national @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , cities must use ward-level indicators to track climate performance in granular detail , enabling targeted interventions . <h> Way Forward for Climate Action in Indian Cities <p> The measures outlined in the previous sections demonstrate a decisive shift in India 's urban climate response . From Heat Action Plans and early warning systems for floods to green bonds , climate budgeting , and risk-informed planning , Indian cities are demonstrating that early locally grounded action can reduce climate-related impacts on health , infrastructure , environment and the economy. 57 The unresolved challenge is to mainstream , scale , and sustain climate action within urban systems and cities . This paper proposes five shifts to achieve these goals . <h> From Reactive Response to Risk-Informed Planning <p> Urban climate risks in India are not solely the result of extreme weather ; they are amplified by planning failures , encroachment on natural systems , and weak enforcement of development controls . Repeated floods and water crises like the 2005 Mumbai floods , 58 the 2015 Chennai floods , 59 and the inundation of Bengaluru 's IT corridors in 202260 have highlighted @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ inadequate stormwater networks in cities increase climate risks . The problem is compounded in coastal cities like Visakhapatnam and Kochi that face additional threats from sea-level rise and cyclones. 61 <p> It is , therefore , imperative to shift from reactive disaster management to proactive , risk-informed urban planning . Odisha 's urban preparedness , with a robust network of 800 multipurpose cyclone shelters and a strong evacuation system , serves as a global reference point . During Cyclone Fani in 2019 , the state evacuated over 1.5 million people within 48 hours , thereby sharply reducing the loss of life compared with earlier cyclones. 62 This state-led model offers a crucial lesson for cities : institutionalised preparedness , early warning systems , and multi-agency coordination can and should be internalised within urban governance . To achieve this , climate components must be incorporated into statutory instruments such as land-use plans and building regulations . <h> From Sector-Specific Delivery to Integrated Urban Systems <p> India 's urban adaptation efforts are hindered by institutional fragmentation . In cities such as Delhi , responsibilities for water supply , drainage , roads , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ overlapping mandates and weak coordination . Emerging models point towards a more integrated way forward . Surat , once devastated by floods , now uses community-based early warning systems and ward-level dashboards to improve preparedness and response. 63 Indore 's decentralised waste management system has earned national recognition for sanitation excellence , including reducing flooding by keeping drains unclogged. 64 Bhubaneswar is beginning to integrate blue-green corridors into its urban planning , treating drainage , lakes , and public open spaces as a single system65 . At the state level , Kerala 's Environmental , Social , and Governance ( ESG ) policy represents a pioneering attempt to embed environmental and social risk considerations into public investment decisions. 66 In the Northeast , Sikkim 's carbon-neutral ambition and Meghalaya 's community forestry programmes show how ecological stewardship and local livelihoods can reinforce adaptation. 67 , 68 <h> From Centralised Strategy to Empowered Local Action <p> Across cities , policymakers increasingly recognise that extreme heat , flooding , water stress , and air pollution have become persistent features of urban life rather than isolated emergencies . Policy attention to urban climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ flagship programmes , including Smart Cities , AMRUT , and Swachh Bharat Urban , 69 have put sustainability , resilience , circularity , and blue-green infrastructure on the agenda of cities . <p> Yet , while national missions and state programmes have expanded the climate agenda for cities , implementation capacity remains uneven . ULBs continue to face constraints in securing stable fiscal transfers , expanding own-source revenues , enhancing technical expertise , and exercising authority to coordinate across sectors and establish permanent city and state-level coordination platforms that align their efforts with state departments , academia , civil society , and the private sector . Designated climate units or cells can be established within ULBs , with clear mandates and authority to coordinate across departments and sectors . Incorporating municipal climate budgets , with spending directly tied to resilience and emissions goals , would improve transparency and outcomes . Implementation effectiveness also depends on addressing gaps in technical capacity , staff continuity , and climate literacy among municipal officials and elected representatives . <h> From Project-Based Funding to Scaled Urban Climate Finance <p> Adaptation and resilience financing remain one @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ While cities like Indore and Pune have successfully issued municipal and green bonds , 70 , 71 most ULBs face limited own-source revenues , weak balance sheets , insufficient capacity for project preparation , and limited access to credit. 72 Scaling adaptation requires access to new instruments , green bonds , pooled financing mechanisms , and schemes such as City Investments to Innovate , Integrate and Sustain ( CITIIS ) 2.0 and the proposed Urban Challenge Fund. 73 , 74 These instruments must be complemented by reforms to property taxation , user charges , pooled borrowing , and climate-linked fiscal transfers to strengthen municipal financial autonomy . Cities also need targeted support to structure technically and financially viable climate projects that can attract market capital . <h> From Compliance Reporting to Outcome-Based Climate Governance <p> Sustained climate action depends on robust measurement , accountability , and the institutional ability to act on evidence . The Climate -- Smart Cities Assessment Framework ( CSCAF ) , developed by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs and the National Institute for Urban Affairs ' Climate Centre for Cities , is an important @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ It assesses cities across 28 indicators , including urban planning , energy , mobility , water , waste , and biodiversity , enabling benchmarking and peer learning . Performance data from cities such as Surat , Indore , Pune , and Visakhapatnam indicate that cities perform strongly when institutions , finance , and data systems are aligned . Continuous tracking can help city governments identify performance gaps and make better decisions about resource allocation . <p> Outcome-based governance must also explicitly account for equity . Climate risks are not evenly distributed within cities . Vulnerability , as defined in recent Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change reports , stems from a combination of greater exposure to hazards and a higher sensitivity to their effects. 75 Gender , age , disability , livelihood source , migration status , and housing conditions determine who is hit hardest . Informal settlements , low-income neighbourhoods , women , older persons , and outdoor workers often face greater exposure to risks and have fewer resources to cope with them , and therefore require prioritisation . Outcomes should reflect who benefits from interventions , not merely aggregate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is thus essential for identifying areas and groups with higher exposure or lower access to services . <p> Transparency and public engagement can strengthen outcome-oriented governance . By making a limited set of outcome indicators publicly available and providing structured mechanisms for citizen feedback and participation , particularly at the ward level , ground-level insights can be generated and residents ' confidence reinforced . <h> Conclusion <p> The evidence presented in this brief points to a clear shift in how Indian cities approach climate action . International commitments under the Paris Agreement , the Sendai Framework , and the SDGs have influenced national priorities . This , in turn , is reflected in national missions , State Action Plans , and urban programmes . At the city level , Climate Action Plans , sectoral reforms , and targeted investments are already underway . Recent messages from the Economic Survey , Union Budget announcements , and the 16th Finance Commission 's recommendations collectively position climate adaptation and resilience not as environmental add-ons , but as core development investments that must be embedded in urban planning , infrastructure delivery , and public @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , will be realised not through declarations , but through everyday urban choices , such as how cities plan land use , prioritise infrastructure , allocate budgets , and manage risk . Going ahead , climate risks must be addressed through risk-informed planning that encompasses land use , infrastructure investment , and building regulations , with urban systems treated as interconnected . <p> The task ahead is straightforward : fiscal transfers , urban investment frameworks , and governance reforms must be aligned with climate outcomes , and cities must be equipped with the authority , capacity , and finance to deliver on these commitments . Climate-ready cities are no longer a policy aspiration ; they are an economic and institutional necessity . <p> Hitesh Vaidya is an urban practitioner , former Director of the National Institute of Urban Affairs , and Former Country Representative of United Nations-Habitat India . <p> Vijaya Venkataraman is an independent consultant in urban development and governance . <p> The authors acknowledge the use of Perplexity Pro 2.87.0 to format the endnotes in this brief . <p> All views expressed in this publication are solely those @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Research Foundation , either in its entirety or its officials and personnel . 
@@138275608 <h> A FRAGMENTED WORLD <p> When G7 leaders gather in ? vian on 15 June , they will confront a postwar order that has run its course . The United Nations , the Bretton Woods institutions , and other pillars of international cooperation -- all founded on the belief that universal rules could underpin global governance -- delivered decades of relative stability and economic integration . But today 's world is too multipolar , too digitally interconnected , and too politically heterogeneous for broad consensus alone to serve as the primary mechanism for managing global affairs . <p> As national interests diverge , economic interdependence is increasingly wielded as an instrument of coercion , giving rise to rival strategic blocs at a moment when global challenges such as climate change , migration , and AI are intensifying faster than existing institutions can respond . While it may be tempting to cling to a fading order or resign ourselves to permanent geopolitical rivalry , what is needed is a transition to a new model of international cooperation grounded in coalition-based governance . <h> Also Read <p> In many respects , this @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . From semiconductor supply chains to climate and security , countries are increasingly cooperating through issue-specific coalitions -- flexible partnerships reflecting the realities of a fragmented yet deeply interconnected world . The question facing the G7 , then , is not whether coalition-based governance will emerge , but whether democracies will shape this transition or allow it to be driven by power politics alone . Few bodies are better positioned to guide the process than the G7 , which combines economic scale , technological capability , institutional capacity , and broadly aligned political values . But that requires rethinking governance accordingly . <p> For starters , policymakers must move beyond the pursuit of universal agreement . Consensus increasingly leads to paralysis , and even when broad agreements are reached , implementation is often inconsistent . The 2015 Paris climate agreement illustrates the problem : while it established shared goals , national commitments vary widely and enforcement remains weak . Similar problems are now evident in digital governance , taxation , trade , and migration policy . <p> Coalition-based governance offers a more practical alternative . Rather than requiring universal agreement @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ while committing to common standards , monitoring mechanisms , and enforcement tools . Participation remains voluntary , but membership comes with responsibilities . <p> AI is a case in point . Countries could form a coalition to establish shared standards for frontier AI systems , common data-governance rules , coordinated oversight of AI supply chains , and safeguards against systemic risks . Access to coalition markets , financial systems , research networks , and digital infrastructure would be contingent on meeting those standards . The same logic could be applied to climate policy , trade , critical minerals , biotechnology , cybersecurity , and financial transparency . <p> Far from abandoning multilateralism , this approach adapts it to today 's multipolar reality . Coalition-based governance offers a more flexible and effective framework for cooperation in a world in which major powers no longer share the same interests , values , or political models . <p> At the same time , governance must become more integrated . Today 's most pressing challenges are deeply interconnected , but governments continue to approach them through bureaucratic silos . This makes no sense . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ technological security . Financial regulation must account for climate change and geopolitical risk . And digital governance must balance innovation and competition with democratic resilience and national security . <p> The G7 could lead this shift by building coalitions around interlinked systemic challenges that require integrated policy responses , such as food , water , and energy security ; AI , employment , and digital human rights ; and climate change , biodiversity loss , and industrial transformation . Bringing together finance ministries , regulators , central banks , security agencies , businesses , and civil-society organisations , these coalitions would align economic , technological , and security priorities rather than merely coordinate policy . <p> Perhaps most importantly , governments must rethink how they define success . For decades , economic output has been the primary measure of performance . But as recent experience has shown , robust GDP growth can coexist with economic insecurity , social fragmentation , political polarisation , declining trust , and environmental degradation . Governments that measure success narrowly tend to govern narrowly . One promising alternative is the SAGE dashboard , which offers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ human flourishing around four factors that have enabled societies to thrive throughout history : solidarity , agency , material gain , and environmental sustainability . Instead of defining success solely in terms of economic output , this framework evaluates whether people enjoy cohesive communities , meaningful agency over their lives , and a healthy environment . <p> No emerging international order will revolve around a single center of power , development model , or set of priorities . In the best case , it will comprise overlapping coalitions focused on different issues and sectors . The challenge is to ensure that what overlaps also reinforces , rather than causing friction , fueling conflict , and perpetuating incoherence . <p> The future of global governance lies in learning how to govern a more diverse and fragmented world . The G7 summit offers a unique opportunity to articulate a coalition-based vision of international cooperation that can expand and evolve to incorporate new partners from the G20 and beyond . In doing so , it can help lay the foundation for a more adaptive and resilient world order . <p> The writer is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ .

@@138285961 <p> The mid-year climate talks in Bonn , Germany , that ended this week failed to make much headway on any contentious issue , but did throw up one interesting proposal . <p> Turkey , which will host the year-ending climate conference COP31 this year , proposed that the world should aim to meet at least a third of its energy needs from electricity by 2035 to reduce emissions . As of now , only about 20% of the world 's final energy consumption is met through electricity . <p> Advertisement <p> Turkey has suggested that all countries agree to adopt this goal as one of the outcomes from the COP31 conference , which it is hosting together with Australia in the Turkish city of Antalya in November . <p> The electrification target , if agreed upon , would be one more addition to several other climate-related global goals that are already in place , the foremost being the temperature targets contained in the Paris Agreement . The 2015 Paris Agreement says the world must strive to limit the rise in global temperatures within 2 degrees Celsius , preferably 1.5 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( Conference of Parties ) climate meetings that are held every year have yielded a few more of these targets . COP28 in Dubai in 2023 , for instance , decided that countries should work towards tripling the global installed capacity of renewable energy by 2030 from its existing levels in 2023 . <p> Advertisement <p> Countries have also endorsed targets for achieving a global net-zero emissions status , for mobilisation of climate finance , and for accelerating the rate of energy efficiency improvements . These are all aimed at reducing the world 's dependence on fossil fuels and speeding up the process of energy transition , which is the only effective long-term solution for climate change . <p> Electrification is at the heart of this energy transition . In fact , a complete energy transition , from fossil fuels such as oil , gas and coal , to cleaner sources such as wind and solar , is not even possible without full electrification . Tracking the electrification rate , therefore , is a good measure of the progress on energy transition . It also encapsulates the enormity of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ electrification challenge <p> Climate change is the result of global warming which is caused by greenhouse gas emissions . Emissions come primarily from burning fossil fuels such as coal , oil , gas and wood , which are the main sources of energy . A solution to the climate crisis , therefore , involves replacing these traditional sources of energy with newer and cleaner sources such as solar , wind , nuclear or hydropower , which have a much smaller carbon footprint . This is the great energy transition that the world has to go through to deal with the climate crisis . <p> It is not immediately obvious , but there is a fundamental difference between fossil fuels and the newer energy sources that have to replace them . <p> Fossil fuels are direct sources of energy . They only require to be burnt to produce energy . Renewables , however , have to be converted into electricity before they can be put to use . <p> Replacing fossil fuels with the cleaner sources means that the only way energy would eventually be available would be in the form @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ every final use of energy would have to be electrified . <p> Considering how ubiquitous electricity has become , and the transformative impact it has had on the world in the last century and a half , it sometimes comes as a surprise that as of now , electricity meets only a small fraction of the world 's total energy needs . According to the International Energy Agency ( IEA ) , electricity accounted for only 21% of the total final energy consumption ( TFEC ) in the year 2025 . In India , the corresponding figure is about 23% , according to government data . <p> TFEC , or FEC , is a measure of energy that is ultimately used . It excludes all the energy that is consumed in producing , transforming or transporting energy itself . The coal that is burnt to produce electricity , or the energy used for refining petroleum , the diesel burnt for transporting fuel trucks , or the transmission and distribution losses in electricity , are not counted in FEC . All these are included in another metric called Total Primary Energy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ total energy available for use . <p> Over the years , the amount of electricity being generated , globally , has increased from about 24 terrawatt-hours ( TWh ) in 2015 to over 32 TWh in 2025 , a rise of nearly 33% . But the share of electricity in FEC has had a more modest rise during this period , from 17.7% in 2015 to 21% in 2025 . <p> This is because a large number of sectors and processes are still difficult to electrify . Shipping and aviation , heavy-duty and long-haul trucks , many high-temperature processes in industries like iron and steel , cement , glass and ceramics , and even many residential needs like heating have remained largely unelectrified . This means these processes still can not run on renewable energy . <h> Staring at a crisis <p> But this is not all . Electricity itself continues to be generated primarily by fossil fuels . In 2025 , only about 42% of all the electricity in the world was generated by non-fossil fuel sources -- renewables , hydro and nuclear -- according to the latest IEA @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Only about 21% of total final energy consumption happens in the form of electricity . And only about 42% of electricity is generated through clean sources . That means that just a little over 8% of the total energy consumed in the world now is clean . After nearly three decades of efforts to promote cleaner fuels , through favourable policies , financial incentives , and technology innovation , more than 90% of the current global use of energy continues to depend on fossil fuels . <p> This is the enormity of the challenge that is not always evident in climate change or energy transition discussions . <p> The road ahead is not smooth . Renewables are expected to continue to expand at a fast rate , no doubt , but the share of electricity in FEC is not projected to increase dramatically . According to the latest estimates from IEA , non-fossils ( renewables plus hydro and nuclear ) are likely to begin producing nearly half of the world 's electricity by 2030 . But the share of electricity in global FEC is expected to go up to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <h> Ambitious electrification target <p> That is why Turkey 's proposal to make efforts to increase it to 35% by 2035 is an ambitious target . The proposal is based on a recent roadmap prepared by the International Renewable Energy Agency ( IRENA ) , which incidentally puts the current electrification level at 23% , slightly higher than IEA 's figure of 21% . <p> IRENA says a 35% electrification rate by 2035 is the minimum needed to entertain any hopes of keeping the world on the 1.5-degrees Celsius pathway . But to achieve that level of electrification , an investment of about $1.2 trillion needs to be pumped into electricity systems every year . A number of other things , including rapid expansion in renewables , and battery storage systems , also need to happen . <p> It is not very clear how the current wars and geopolitical tensions would affect this process of energy transition . <p> Greater uncertainty in supplies of fossil fuels , and rising oil prices , may force the countries to give a greater push for renewable deployment , including decentralised systems . But @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ budgets available for investing in new technologies and infrastructure . Countries might be tempted to use whatever energy source is easily available to them , regardless of its climate impact .

@@138287017 <h> Why India 's youth deserve a seat at the decision-making table <p> By Abhinav Narayan Jha <p> By all demographic measures , India is a young nation . Nearly 65 per cent of its population is below the age of 35 , and the country 's median age hovers around 28 years . Political leaders across party lines proudly refer to India 's youth as its greatest asset , its demographic dividend , and the driving force of a rising global power . Yet , there is an uncomfortable reality that rarely finds space in political speeches : while young Indians dominate the population , they remain conspicuously absent from the institutions that make decisions on their behalf . India may be one of the youngest democracies in terms of population , but its Parliament and Legislative Assemblies tell a completely different story . The contradiction is glaring . According to available data from the 18th Lok Sabha elected in 2024 , fewer than one in ten Members of Parliament are between 25 and 40 years of age . The average age of the House is approximately 56 years @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> The question , therefore , is straightforward : how can a democracy claim to represent its people when its largest demographic group remains significantly underrepresented in its highest decision-making bodies ? It is a question of democratic legitimacy . Historically , the situation was far more encouraging . In the first Lok Sabha constituted in 1952 , nearly 30 per cent of MPs were aged 40 years or below . Seven decades later , despite India 's youthful population growing substantially , youth representation in Parliament has sharply declined to around 10 per cent . Instead of becoming more inclusive and accessible , Indian politics appears to have become increasingly exclusive . Political parties across the ideological spectrum frequently celebrate young voters . Election campaigns are designed around social media outreach , youth conventions , campus interactions , digital engagement and promises of employment and opportunity . Every political party understands the electoral value of young voters . However , when it comes to distributing party tickets , leadership responsibilities and positions of influence , the enthusiasm for youth participation suddenly diminishes . Young Indians are encouraged to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The barriers are both visible and invisible . Electoral politics increasingly demands substantial financial resources , extensive organisational networks and years of political patronage . For first-generation aspirants , the path is extraordinarily difficult . This brings us to another uncomfortable truth : dynastic politics . A significant proportion of younger politicians entering Parliament and Assemblies today belong to established political families . While many of these leaders are capable and deserving in their own right , their presence highlights a deeper structural issue . <p> For every young leader with a political surname , thousands of equally talented young Indians without such advantages remain excluded from the system . The result is a political ecosystem where youth representation exists , but genuine youth inclusion remains limited . Representation should mean creating opportunities for talented young Indians from diverse social , economic and regional backgrounds to participate in governance . <p> The implications of this democratic deficit are profound . The twenty-first century presents challenges fundamentally different from those faced by previous generations . Artificial intelligence , cyber security , climate change , digital governance , start-up ecosystems , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ technological disruptions are shaping the lives of millions of young Indians . Yet the voices most directly affected by these issues remain insufficiently represented in legislative discussions . A Parliament that lacks youth perspectives risks creating policies that are disconnected from contemporary realities . This does not mean experience is unimportant . Governance requires wisdom that often comes with experience . But democracy functions best when experience and innovation coexist . The challenge becomes even more evident at the state level . <p> Youth wings exist within almost every major political party , but they often function as mobilisation platforms rather than genuine leadership pipelines . Many young leaders spend years organising events , managing campaigns and mobilising supporters without receiving meaningful opportunities to contest elections . This creates frustration , disengagement and cynicism . When politics appears inaccessible , talented individuals increasingly look elsewhere . Entrepreneurs build start-ups . Professionals join corporations . Scholars enter academia . Few see electoral politics as a realistic avenue for public service . <p> The solution is not symbolic tokenism . The solution lies in structural reform . Political parties should voluntarily allocate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of 40 . Internal party elections must become more transparent and merit-based . Campaign finance reforms should reduce the overwhelming financial barriers that discourage young entrants . Structured mentorship programmes should connect experienced legislators with emerging leaders . <p> Equally important is the creation of institutional pathways . Youth Parliaments , student legislatures , public policy fellowships and civic leadership initiatives should not remain ceremonial exercises . They must become genuine training grounds that connect young citizens with real political opportunities . India , despite possessing one of the youngest populations globally , risks lagging behind if it fails to address this imbalance . <p> The responsibility does not rest solely with political parties . Young Indians themselves must move beyond political spectatorship . Democracy can not be strengthened merely through social media commentary . It requires active participation , organisational engagement , public service and leadership . However , participation can flourish only when opportunities exist . The real question is whether India 's political establishment is ready to trust them with it . For decades , political leaders have referred to young people as the future of India @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ youth are not simply the future . They are the present . They are taxpayers , entrepreneurs , innovators , students , professionals , farmers , workers and voters . They are shaping the country 's economy , society and global reputation every day . Surely , they deserve a greater role in shaping its laws as well . If India truly believes that its youth are its greatest strength , then the time has come to offer them not just a voice in election campaigns , but a seat in Parliament and Legislative Assemblies where the nation 's future is ultimately decided . <p> The writer is an advocate and columnist ; Views presented are personal .

@@138287281 <p> As we navigate the second quarter of 2026 , the intersection of international trade and environmental jurisprudence has reached a state of critical friction . The global community is no longer debating " if " climate change will disrupt trade , but " how " the law should mitigate the resulting economic disparities . The definitive implementation of the European Union 's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism ( CBAM ) has fundamentally altered the landscape , effectively imposing carbon-linked tariffs on Global South exports . However , a profound legal paradox remains : while the Global North uses trade sticks to enforce decarbonization , it continues to hoard the " Green DNA " the proprietary intellectual property ( IP ) necessary for that transition . <p> This creates what can be analytically termed a " Regulatory Pincer Movement . " Developing nations are penalized for high-carbon production , yet the patented technologies required for mitigation such as high-efficiency green hydrogen electrolyzers and carbon-sequestration modules remain locked behind the exorbitant paywalls of the TRIPS Agreement . The " Green Patent Bottleneck " is thus not merely a commercial hurdle ; it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ private rights of inventors with the collective survival of the planet . <p> II . The Jurisprudential Mirage of Article 66.2 : A Critique of Voluntarism <p> An analytical critique of the current IP regime must begin with the systemic collapse of the " Grand Bargain " of 1994 . Under Article 66.2 of the TRIPS Agreement , developed nations hold a hard legal obligation to provide incentives for technology transfer to Least Developed Countries ( LDCs ) . 1 In the 2026 reality , however , Article 66.2 has devolved into a " dead letter . " Developed states fulfill their reporting requirements by citing private-sector " voluntary " licenses agreements that are commercially prohibitive for South Asian manufacturers and rarely include the high-end innovation needed to meet 2026 emission standards . <p> This " Voluntarism Fallacy " ignores the structural power imbalance inherent in IP negotiations . By delegating the state 's obligation to the private sector , the international community has allowed " Climate Capitalism " to supersede " Climate Justice . " From a South Asian perspective , this is a breach of the fundamental principles @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ protection of IP should contribute to the " dissemination and transfer of technology . " 2 When technology transfer becomes an act of corporate charity rather than a statutory mandate , the developmental goals of the Global South are effectively subverted . <p> To dismantle this bottleneck , legal scholarship must pivot toward a " Climate Emergency Waiver " that transcends the logic of the 2001 Doha Declaration on Public Health. 3 While the Doha model proved that the WTO could prioritize " Public Health over Patents " during a crisis , the climate emergency presents a more complex " Interface Problem . " Unlike a vaccine , " Green Tech " is not a single product but a convergence of hardware , software , and industrial processes . <p> Therefore , a unique legal argument must be raised . In 2026 , Climate-Essential Technologies ( CETs ) must be recognized as possessing a " Jus Cogens " character . These are obligations so fundamental to the preservation of the human race that they should override standard commercial IP protections . Under the " Public Interest " exception of Article @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ threat of climate change constitutes a " State of Necessity , " justifying a broad , time-bound waiver on IPR for technologies related to renewable energy and carbon mitigation. 4 <p> IV . The Trade Secret Trap : The Invisible Patent Wall <p> The final , and perhaps most insidious , barrier to green technology is the " Trade Secret Trap . " In 2026 , many green innovations are no longer shielded by patents which eventually expire and require public disclosure but by perpetual trade secrets under Article 39. 5 For a South Asian manufacturer , having a patent waiver for a solid-state battery is functionally useless without the proprietary " know-how " of the chemical stabilization process . <p> An analytical solution requires the WTO to adopt a " Forced Interoperability Standard " for CETs . The argument is simple : if a technology is marketed as " Green " to benefit from carbon credits or green subsidies in the Global North , its fundamental " know-how " must be contributed to a Global Green Commons . This would transform Article 39 from a shield for " Exclusive @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " The goal is not to abolish profit , but to prevent a scenario where a single corporation 's trade secret becomes a bottleneck for the entire planet 's survival . <p> V. The Enforcement Paradox : BNS 2023 and Digital Forensics <p> One must also view this through the lens of domestic enforcement and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita ( BNS ) 2023 . In the 2026 landscape , " electronic records " and digital forensics are central to proving IP infringement6 . If the Global North continues to deny technology transfer , we may see a rise in " Compulsory Reverse Engineering . " <p> If an Indian firm utilizes an AI-driven tool to " guess " a trade secret for carbon capture , does it constitute a criminal act under the new BNS framework , or is it a justified act of " Climate Survival " ? By failing to provide a legal channel for tech transfer , the TRIPS Agreement is inadvertently pushing developing nations toward a digital " Gray Market " for innovation , where the line between " theft " and " necessity " becomes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ VI . Reclaiming the South Asian Developmental Space <p> The " Green Patent Bottleneck " represents the ultimate test of technological sovereignty . The 2026 Amendments to the IT Rules and the broader evolution of the IPR regime must reflect a simple truth : you can not tax the poor for their carbon while locking the tools to reduce it in a safe. 7 <p> A Climate TRIPS Waiver is not a radical demand for a handout ; it is a corrective measure to restore the " Grand Bargain " of international trade . If the WTO can not evolve from a protector of R&amp;D rents into a facilitator of global resilience , it risks total delegitimization in the eyes of the Global South . 
@@138287487 <h> At the heart of urban sprawl lies a particular way of seeing land : not as a shared trust between generations , but as a commodity to be bought , sold , and exploited for maximum short-term gain <p> DR SYED ZAFFAR <p> On the outskirts of many of our towns and cities , the story is written not in policy documents but in concrete . Where there were once paddy fields , orchards , and wetlands , there now stand clusters of boxy structures -- half-finished commercial complexes , cramped colonies , and narrow lanes choked with parked vehicles . The sky , once open and generous , is increasingly framed by a tangle of rooftops and dangling wires . This slow , relentless spread of the city into the countryside has a name : urban sprawl . <p> Urban sprawl is often mistaken for development . To the casual eye , more buildings , more shops , and more traffic appear as signs of progress . But when this growth is unplanned , unregulated , and insensitive to the environment or local needs , it becomes a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ community . It is development without direction -- a city that grows in all directions but never truly grows up . <p> In our own context , we have watched this pattern unfold over the last few decades . Villages that once stood at a respectful distance from city centres are now swallowed by expanding municipal limits . Agricultural land is parcelled and sold , wetlands are filled and forgotten , and hill slopes are cut into terraces of concrete . The promise is always the same : better housing , better connectivity , better opportunities . The reality , too often , is overcrowded neighbourhoods with poor drainage , little greenery , inadequate public transport , and an infrastructure straining under pressure it was never designed to bear . <p> Land as a commodity , not a trust <p> At the heart of urban sprawl lies a particular way of seeing land : not as a shared trust between generations , but as a commodity to be bought , sold , and exploited for maximum short-term gain . When land becomes merely an investment , its other roles -- @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ against floods , as a habitat for birds and wildlife , as a keeper of cultural memory -- fade into the background . <p> This mentality has reshaped the edges of our cities . Builders and brokers move faster than planners ; layouts appear before infrastructure ; permissions are regularised after the fact , if at all . The logic is simple : build first , ask questions later . In this race for quick profit , the long-term public interest is the first casualty . <p> For a region like ours , where arable land is limited and ecological balance is fragile , this is especially dangerous . Every orchard turned into a gated colony , every wetland converted into a parking lot , narrows the space available for future generations to grow food , recharge groundwater , and breathe clean air . We are trading permanent assets for temporary comfort -- and too often , for someone else 's profit . <p> The invisible cost of concrete <p> Urban sprawl carries costs that are rarely reflected in sale deeds or property advertisements . These costs are paid slowly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> There is a strain on basic services . When houses and shopping complexes mushroom on the outskirts without proper planning , water supply , sewage systems , solid waste management , and roads are perpetually playing catch-up . Tankers become a way of life ; septic tanks overflow into open drains ; garbage piles up in empty plots or along streams . Residents pay twice -- once for the property , and again in the form of poor quality of life . <p> Sprawl deepens dependence on private vehicles . Low-density colonies scattered across the periphery make efficient public transport difficult to run . People are pushed towards cars and two-wheelers for even the smallest errands . The result is predictable : longer commutes , more traffic congestion , higher fuel consumption , and rising air pollution . What looks like quiet suburban living on a brochure turns into hours lost in traffic and an ever-present haze on the horizon . <p> The environmental impact is severe . Wetlands that could have absorbed excess rainwater are filled , increasing the risk of flooding . Green cover is replaced @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ effect -- cities becoming significantly warmer than their surrounding rural areas . Streams are encroached upon or turned into open drains , depriving both people and ecosystems of clean flowing water . <p> These are not abstract concerns . We have already seen how extreme weather events , from heavy rainfall to sudden heatwaves , expose the weaknesses of our built environment . Urban sprawl , by eroding natural buffers and overloading fragile infrastructure , turns these climate shocks into disasters . <p> A community without a centre <p> Beyond the physical and environmental impacts , urban sprawl quietly reshapes the social fabric . Traditional neighbourhoods in the core city , with their mixed-use streets , shared courtyards , and walkable markets , fostered a sense of belonging . People met each other not only in moments of crisis or ceremony , but in the everyday rhythm of life -- at the bakery , the mosque , the local shop , the school gate . <p> The sprawling peripheries , by contrast , often produce fragmented communities . Residential colonies are cut off from workplaces and markets . Public spaces @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at all , while vast areas are devoted to roads and parking . Social interaction shifts indoors , behind gates and guard rooms . The city becomes a series of pockets rather than a shared space . <p> This fragmentation matters . A society where neighbours do not know each other is more vulnerable to crime , to misinformation , to apathy in the face of collective problems . When public life shrinks , so does the space for democratic engagement . The urban resident becomes primarily a consumer , less a citizen . <p> Planning on paper , chaos on the ground <p> Urban planners in our region are not unaware of these dangers . Master plans are drafted , maps are drawn , and zoning regulations are written . On paper , the future of our cities often looks orderly : clearly demarcated residential , commercial , and green zones ; protected wetlands ; provisions for public transport and open spaces . <p> The problem lies in the gulf between plan and practice . Regulations are bent under pressure , violators are regularised instead of penalised , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the master plan is treated as a suggestion rather than a binding framework . <p> This gap between vision and enforcement is a symptom of a deeper malaise : a lack of political will to treat urban land as a public trust rather than a private jackpot . When encroachment is rewarded and violations go unpunished , sprawl becomes not an accident but an outcome . <p> Rethinking what it means to grow <p> If urban sprawl is not true development , what does genuine growth look like ? It begins with a different set of questions . Instead of asking , " How far can the city spread ? " we must ask , " How well can the city live within its limits ? " <p> One answer lies in densification with dignity -- making better use of land within existing urban boundaries by improving infrastructure , upgrading older neighbourhoods , and promoting mixed-use , walkable areas . A city that grows upwards in a planned , humane way can reduce pressure to grow endlessly outwards . <p> Another answer is to strengthen smaller towns and rural centres @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , swollen urban core . When education , healthcare , and employment are more evenly distributed , the push towards speculative construction on the city 's edges can be reduced . <p> Crucially , ecological considerations must be non-negotiable . Wetlands , floodplains , forests , and agricultural belts can not be treated as " wasteland " waiting to be built upon . They are infrastructure of another kind -- natural systems that protect us from the very disasters our concrete invites . <p> Citizens as custodians , not bystanders <p> Confronting urban sprawl is not the task of planners and politicians alone . Residents , too , have a role to play in shaping the future of their cities . This begins with refusing to see land purely through the lens of personal gain . <p> When we purchase property in clear violation of zoning rules , or look the other way as wetlands are filled for convenience , we become silent partners in a long-term robbery -- stealing from our own children 's future . Legal awareness , public pressure , and civic engagement are essential tools . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ push for better public transport instead of endless road-widening , and protect local green spaces . Media and civil society can highlight the cumulative impact of seemingly small encroachments , rather than waking up only when a crisis strikes . <p> Educating young people about the environmental and social costs of unplanned growth can also shift attitudes over time . If the next generation learns to value rivers more than ring roads , wetlands more than warehouses , then the political space for responsible planning will widen . <p> Choosing a different horizon <p> Urban sprawl often feels inevitable , as if the city were a creeping tide that nothing can hold back . But cities are not forces of nature ; they are choices , made and unmade every day by policies , markets , and collective decisions . <p> We stand at a moment when those choices carry unusual weight . Climate change is intensifying , water resources are under strain , and land conflicts are rising . Continuing on the path of unplanned expansion is not merely inefficient ; it is reckless . <p> The question before @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they already are -- but how they will grow , and at whose expense . Will we allow the logic of quick profit to dictate the shape of our horizon , or will we insist that development be measured not only in square feet built but in lives improved , ecosystems preserved , and futures safeguarded ? <p> To resist urban sprawl is not to resist progress . It is to insist that progress be wise , just , and sustainable . It is to claim the right to a city that is more than a collection of concrete blocks -- a city that remembers its rivers and orchards , honours its communities , and leaves room for those who will inherit it after we are gone . <p> In the end , the battle against sprawl is a battle over imagination . Can we imagine a future in which growth does not mean endless spread , in which the countryside is not treated as mere real estate , and in which the city is a living organism rather than a consuming machine ? Our answer will shape the map @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ will see when they look up from the streets they call home . <p> ( Author is PhD in Public Administration and a Columnist ) <p> Subscribe to our Newsletter ! @@138287489 <h> The Vanishing Taxonomists : A Silent Threat to Biodiversity Conservation <h> The conservation of biodiversity begins with knowing what exists . Taxonomists are the custodians of that knowledge <p> OSMAN JAVID <p> Deep within the forests , alpine meadows , wetlands , and mountain landscapes of the Himalayas exists a world that remains largely unknown . Thousands of species of insects , plants , fungi , and other organisms are yet to be discovered , described , and documented . Yet , at a time when biodiversity is under unprecedented pressure from climate change , habitat degradation , and human activities , a less-discussed crisis is unfolding : the alarming decline of taxonomists . <p> Taxonomy , often referred to as the science of naming , identifying , and classifying organisms , forms the foundation of biodiversity research . Before a species can be conserved , studied , or protected , it must first be recognised and scientifically described . Taxonomists are the individuals who perform this crucial task . However , their numbers are steadily declining , creating a significant gap in our understanding of the natural world @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's megadiverse countries , harbouring an extraordinary variety of life across its ecosystems . Yet a substantial portion of its biodiversity remains unexplored . The Himalayan region , including the Kashmir Valley , is particularly rich in endemic and unique species . Every year , researchers continue to discover species new to science from these mountains , suggesting that countless more remain hidden . The shortage of trained taxonomists has become a major bottleneck in documenting this biological wealth . <p> Many young researchers are increasingly drawn towards modern disciplines such as molecular biology , biotechnology , artificial intelligence , and genomics , often perceiving taxonomy as a traditional field with limited opportunities . Consequently , fewer students are choosing careers in taxonomy , and the expertise accumulated over decades is gradually diminishing . <p> Field-based taxonomy is neither easy nor glamorous . It demands patience , perseverance , and extensive travel to remote locations . Taxonomists often spend weeks or even months conducting surveys in dense forests , rugged mountains , wetlands , and other difficult terrains . Harsh weather conditions , logistical challenges , and concerns regarding personal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . In regions like Kashmir , the challenges are even greater . <p> The valley 's rich biodiversity is spread across remote mountain ranges , high-altitude grasslands , and inaccessible forests . Many areas remain insufficiently surveyed due to difficult terrain and limited scientific expeditions . As a result , numerous species may still await discovery , while others could disappear before they are ever documented . <p> The implications of this decline extend far beyond academic research . Without proper taxonomic expertise , biodiversity assessments become incomplete , conservation planning becomes less effective , and invasive species may go unnoticed . Policymakers and conservation agencies rely on accurate species identification to make informed decisions . A species that remains unknown can not be protected . <p> The urgency becomes even more pronounced in the face of climate change . Rapid environmental shifts are altering species distributions across the Himalayas . Scientists are already observing changes in flowering patterns , insect emergence , and habitat suitability . To understand these changes , baseline biodiversity data are essential , and such data can only be generated through systematic taxonomic research . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tools have opened new possibilities for biodiversity exploration . However , these technologies can not replace traditional taxonomy . Instead , they should complement the expertise of trained taxonomists who understand species morphology , ecology , and evolutionary relationships . <p> Addressing this challenge requires a coordinated effort . Universities and research institutions must strengthen taxonomic training programmes . Greater funding should be allocated for biodiversity surveys and species inventories . Young scientists should be encouraged through fellowships , career opportunities , and field-based research support . <p> Equally important is raising public awareness about the crucial role taxonomists play in understanding and conserving nature . Kashmir , often celebrated for its scenic beauty , also possesses immense biological richness . Yet much of this natural heritage remains undocumented . If the decline in taxonomists continues , countless species may remain unknown , and valuable ecological knowledge may be lost forever . <p> The conservation of biodiversity begins with knowing what exists . Taxonomists are the custodians of that knowledge . Their declining numbers represent not merely a scientific concern but a conservation crisis . @@138295642 <h> The Destruction of Reason and the Rise of Ecofascism in the United States <p> Necropolis in Novi Travnik , Bosnia and Herzegovina , commemorating partisans who died fighting in the anti-Nazi War . More than a mere oxymoron , ecofascism is the ecology of exterminism . <p> In 1953 , in The Destruction of Reason , Georg Luk ? cs indicated that irrationalism was a product of capitalism , deeply connected to the material interests of the ruling class and the imperialist stage of the global system . He explained that in opposition to Marxism , historical-materialist analysis , and revolutionary socialist movements , bourgeois philosophy ( e.g. , Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling , Arthur Schopenhauer , Friedrich Nietzsche , Henri Bergson , Martin Heidegger , and Carl Schmitt ) had shifted to nonscientific , antirationalist , and skeptical analyses , asserting the preeminence of the **26;1119;TOOLONG , instincts , intuition , myths , and vitalistic life principles , as well as a deep social pessimism , over critical-dialectical reason.3 This irrationalism rendered the world meaningless , constituting a nihilism and skepticism that permeated bourgeois society , reinforcing its ideological and class domination and defending its exterminist actions . He explained that in the United States the " ruling class managed , particularly during the imperialist era , to have the democratic forms so effectively preserved due to having a constitution that ' was democratic from the start ' that by democratically legal means , it achieved a dictatorship of monopoly capitalism at least as firm as that which Adolf Hitler set up with tyrannic procedures . " 5 <p> He detailed the coordinated structure of the capitalist state @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ was created by the Presidential prerogative , the Supreme Court 's authority in constitutional questions , the finance monopoly over the Press , radio , etc. , electioneering costs , which successfully prevented really democratic parties from springing up beside the two parties of monopoly capitalism , and lastly the use of terroristic devices ( the lynching system ) . And this democracy could , in substance , realize everything sought by Hitler without needing to break with democracy formally . In addition , there was the incomparably broader and more solid economic basis of monopoly capitalism.6 <p> Luk ? cs indicated that the Cold War was " state-managed from Washington , " employing " the ' free world ' ideology , " which must be recognized as " a part of fascism , " to justify its imperialist ambitions in " defence of capitalism and capitalist ' freedom . , dramatically intensified and increased its impacts on nature @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ which was accompanied by the global expansion of oil production , the advent of the nuclear age , and the revolution
