@@138551785 <h> Bangladesh in the Indo-Pacific : An Analysis of the Interim Government 's Foreign Policy <h> Bangladesh in the Indo-Pacific : An Analysis of the Interim Government 's Foreign Policy <p> In August 2024 , Bangladesh 's 15-year-old Awami League government was toppled after mass protests across the country . The interim government that replaced it held power for nearly one and a half years before the long-awaited elections in February 2026 secured a victory for the Bangladesh Nationalist Party ( BNP ) -led coalition . Appointed only to administer constitutional reforms and steer the country towards a democratic election , the interim regime under Chief Advisor Muhammad Yunus had , by then , stepped well beyond its domestic duties to pursue foreign policy . The engineered shifts in Bangladesh 's engagement with its top bilateral economic partners -- Japan , the US , China , and India -- not only affected its prospects but redefined its role in the Indo-Pacific region , especially as its Indo-Pacific Outlook of 2023 was also withdrawn from the public domain . This paper assesses how the interim government reshaped Bangladesh 's foreign policy with these nations and the impact this had on the country 's strategic and development prospects in the Indo-Pacific . <h> Introduction <p> Bangladesh occupies a strategic geographical position in the Indo-Pacific region at the apex of the Bay of Bengal , near the confluence of the Indian and Pacific Oceans . It overlooks important shipping routes traversing this maritime space and serves as a maritime gateway for landlocked Nepal , Bhutan , and Northeast India , which form its hinterland . Bangladesh is thus an attractive investment destination and a strategic trading partner for extra-regional powers that seek access to South Asian markets and want to secure a presence in the region . <p> Bangladesh 's hydrocarbon blocks in the Bay of Bengal further enhance its value for the world 's largest economies , as they seek uninterrupted fuel supply in an energy-insecure global environment . Its rapidly growing economy , interest in infrastructure development , and a stable government for over one and a half decades added to its potential . Its development is largely contingent on foreign trade and the receipt of developmental loans and grants from external sources. a , 1 <p> Given the criticality of bilateral partnerships , the former Awami League government in Bangladesh under Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina pursued a " Diplomacy of Balance " in its engagement with prominent nations. 2 This term was not formally defined but was an interpretation of the country 's former mandate of ' Friendship towards all , malice toward none , ' frequently used in policy documents during the Hasina era , including the 2023 Indo-Pacific Outlook ( IPO ) that outlined the country 's roles and interests in this geopolitical space . The IPO was a policy of political nonalignment , with reciprocal partnerships with Indo-Pacific countries vital for Dhaka 's economic prosperity and development . <p> In principle , Bangladesh did not overtly align with any partner and maintained friendly relations with all . The core objective was to preserve its autonomy while actively forging ties in a globalised world , so as to advance its national economic and development interests and aspirations . On paper , this helped Bangladesh secure mutually beneficial projects from prospective investors , while retaining the autonomy to select its strategic partners . In practice , it required considerable diplomatic finesse to sustain functional ties with all of Dhaka 's partners , despite their distinct strategic interests and sensitivities , alongside its own priorities. 3 As a result , the Awami League years were mostly marked by close bilateral partnerships with partner countries , even competing ones , such as the United States ( US ) and China in the Indo-Pacific . <p> This balancing exercise was reflected in multiple developmental projects in the country and in vision statements , such as the IPO . However , one of the strongest criticisms against the former Hasina government was its over-alignment with India . Consequently , the interim government headed by Chief Advisor Muhammad Yunus , which replaced the Hasina regime in 2024 , prioritised distancing itself as far as possible from its predecessor 's policies , including shifts in certain foreign policies . Dhaka 's foreign partnerships were thus revised by an unelected government primarily appointed to stabilise the country and steer it towards a democratic election . These changes have strong implications for its development and future role in the Indo-Pacific , which the newly elected Bangladesh Nationalist Party ( BNP ) government must now navigate . <p> This paper assesses how the interim government reshaped Bangladesh 's foreign policy with select Indo-Pacific partner countries and the impact this had on the country 's regional position . It analyses in detail Dhaka 's relations with the US , Japan , and India , countries that consistently rank among Bangladesh 's top ten trading and development partners . China , also one of the main partners , is considered as well ; although Beijing opposes the Indo-Pacific concept as a " containment strategy , " 4 most interpretations , strategies , and visions of the region have a stated or latent China component , given the country 's palpable presence . <p> This paper has three objectives : first , to understand Bangladesh 's economic dependence on these countries and how the Awami League sustained its ' Diplomacy of Balance ' with them via the IPO 2023 ; second , to assess the shifts by the Bangladesh interim government 's ties with these nations ; and third , to evaluate how these changes will affect its future position in the Indo-Pacific . <h> Vital Bilateral Partnerships and the ' Diplomacy of Balance ' <p> According to the 2025 Forbes list , the US , China , Japan , and India rank among the world 's top five economies. 5 To illustrate Bangladesh 's dependence on these countries , it is necessary to assess their development assistanceb and bilateral trade . Regarding the former , project aid receives the most funding ( see Figure 1 ) from the development partners , as their interest in constructing connectivity links in the Bay of Bengal region aligns with Bangladesh 's infrastructural needs. 6 In FY 2023 -- 24 , project aid constituted 77.2 percent of Bangladesh 's foreign aid. 7 <p> Source : Author 's own , based on data from the Government of Bangladesh. 9 <p> Japan provides Bangladesh with Official Development Assistance ( ODA ) through the Japan International Cooperation Agency ( JICA ) . Since 1971 , it has committed nearly US$32.62 billion in the form of project aid , food aid , and commodity aid through grants , loans , and technical assistance . Dhaka has also received about US$910 million in budgetary support from Tokyo to mitigate the macroeconomic crisis caused by the COVID-19 pandemic , the Russia -- Ukraine war , and other factors . As of 1 July 2025 , 78 Japanese ODA-assisted projects were under implementation in Bangladesh . Japanese project aid has been utilised for infrastructure , energy , and industrial projects , notable among which are the Matarbari Ultra Super Critical Coal-Fired Power project , Dhaka Mass Rapid Transit Development Project , Matarbari Port Development Project ( Bangladesh 's first deep-sea port ) , Jamuna Railway Bridge construction project , and Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport Expansion Project . Japan 's Sumitomo Corporation , along with JICA and the Bangladesh Economic Zones Authority , operates the Bangladesh Special Economic Zone ( SEZ ) in Narayanganj. 10 This is the country 's first SEZ led by a Japanese company , with infrastructure built to international standards. 11 <p> China is also deeply invested in Bangladesh 's development . Dhaka became a member of Beijing 's flagship Belt and Road Initiative ( BRI ) in 2016 , c as a critical node , due to its geographic positioning and potential . Bangladesh is the second-largest recipient of Chinese loans , receiving an estimated US$10 billion in 2021. 12 Transportation projects form a focus area , and Beijing constructed 12 roads , 21 bridges , and 27 power plants in Bangladesh between 2016 ( when Dhaka joined the BRI ) and 2023. 13 Important initiatives include assistance in building parts of the Chattogram and Mongla seaports and the Payra deep-sea port. 14 China also helped construct the Padma Multipurpose Bridge , 15 which is expected to boost Bangladesh 's Gross Domestic Product ( GDP ) by 1.2 percent , 16 and has reportedly generated 550,000 new jobs. 17 The Padma Bridge is noteworthy because it facilitates easy movement between the eastern and western parts of the country without having to cross the Padma River , which is particularly torrential in the monsoon . In addition , China , in partnership with the Bangladesh Economic Zones Authority , is developing the Chinese Industrial Economic Zone in Anwara Upazila , Chattogram , to help Chinese manufacturing investments , given the increased US tariffs on Chinese products. 18 Apart from civilian infrastructure , Beijing has also constructed Bangladesh 's first submarine base , the BNS Sheikh Hasina , on the coast of Cox 's Bazaar. 19 <p> Neighbouring India has also extended support for various development-oriented initiatives in Bangladesh through Lines of Credit ( LOCs ) , Grants-in-Aid for projects , as well as support for ' High Impact Community Development Projects ' d and capacity-building programmes . Since 2014 , India has extended two LOCs to Bangladesh that totalled US$6.5 billion. 20 It is especially keen to develop transport connectivity with Bangladesh , especially along the historical routes that were closed after India 's partition in 1947 and the India -- Pakistan 1965 war . It has invested in several connectivity projects linking cities in both countries , notably three passenger trains -- the Maitree Express ( Kolkata -- Dhaka ) , the Bandhan Express ( Kolkata -- Khulna ) , and the Mital Express ( Siliguri -- Dhaka ) . The two countries have also developed the India -- Bangladesh Protocol Routes , which are inland waterways for trade . New Delhi has constructed the Maitri Setu as well -- a bridge over the Feni River that connects Sabroom in Tripura , India , to Ramgarh in Chittagong or Chattogram , Bangladesh , leading to the Chattogram port . However , the Akhaura ( Bangladesh ) -- Agartala ( India ) rail link was stalled due to the regime change in Dhaka , as well as the development work in the Mongla Port. 21 <p> Apart from transport , India has also invested in energy projects . It has helped establish the Maitree Super Thermal Power Project ; constructed the India -- Bangladesh Friendship Pipeline that carries diesel from Assam , India , to the northern districts of Rajshahi and Rangpur in Bangladesh ; 22 and supported the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant , Bangladesh 's first nuclear project , built with Russian assistance. 23 <p> Between 1971 and 2022 , the US invested over US$8 billion in Bangladesh , making it the largest recipient of US assistance in Asia . Rather than building connectivity infrastructure , Washington 's funds were utilised for a variety of enterprises , including support for sustainable agriculture , food security , modernising small-scale farming , strengthening the trade and business environment , climate change adaptation , conserving biodiversity , public health and education , disaster management , and promoting democracy. 24 However , following a directive from the Donald Trump administration elected in 2025 , the US Agency for International Development ( USAID ) was officially closed , with more than 80 percent of its programmes being cancelled as of March 2025 , and the remainder absorbed by the State Department. 25 In Bangladesh , this led to the closure of 55 out of 59 ongoing projects , job losses for 50,000 professionals , and loss of development assistance worth US$700 million. 26 <p> These countries also rank high in terms of trade with Bangladesh . In FY 2023 -- 24 ( the latest available data ) , the US was Dhaka 's largest export destination , followed by India in the eighth place and Japan in the ninth place . Despite its high volume of trade with Bangladesh , China does not feature among the top 10 export destinations ( see Table 2 ) . <p> Source : Author 's calculations , based on Government of Bangladesh data. 27 <p> However , China is Bangladesh 's largest import source , followed by India . The US and Japan ranked sixth and seventh ( see Table 3 ) . <p> Table 3 : Bangladesh 's Top Ten Bilateral Import Sources in 2023 -- 24 <p> Rank <p> Country <p> Value in Million TK <p> Percentage of Total Trade <p> 1 <p> China <p> 1,262,416 <p> 23.10 <p> 2 <p> India <p> 565,696 <p> 13.49 <p> 3 <p> Indonesia <p> 412,031 <p> 6.05 <p> 4 <p> Malaysia <p> 309,411 <p> 4.40 <p> 5 <p> Hong Kong <p> 301,769 <p> 3.31 <p> 6 <p> US <p> 212,365 <p> 3.23 <p> 7 <p> Japan <p> 187,723 <p> 2.27 <p> 8 <p> Canada <p> 146,471 <p> 2.01 <p> 9 <p> Australia <p> 136,705 <p> 1.57 <p> 10 <p> Korea <p> 3,660,820 <p> 1.46 <p> Source : Author 's calculations , based on Government of Bangladesh data. 28 <p> Bangladesh 's trade patterns with the US , China , Japan , and India reveal a structural asymmetry . The US remains its largest export market , while the former 's role as an import source is comparatively limited . As a Least Developed Country ( LDC ) , Bangladesh benefits from duty-free or preferential market access for its garments in the US , helping it become the world 's second-largest apparel exporter after China. 29 While it does not have a formal Generalised System of Preferences ( GSP ) arrangement with the US , it relies on these preferential conditions for its Ready-made Garments ( RMG ) , the backbone of its economy . While Bangladesh will lose these benefits once it graduates from an LDC to a developing nation , as planned in 2026 , 166 World Trade Organization ( WTO ) members have agreed to extend it duty-free market access until 2029 . Currently , around 73 percent of Bangladesh 's RMG exports enjoy this privilege. 30 <p> Since China , as mentioned above , is Bangladesh 's largest import source , but not among its top export destinations , Dhaka is dependent on Beijing 's supply chains rather than access to its market . India occupies an intermediate position , emerging as Bangladesh 's second-largest import source while being a modest export destination , reflecting a persistent trade imbalance . Japan 's trade profile is comparatively balanced , with moderate shares on both the export and import sides . Collectively , these patterns highlight Bangladesh 's reliance on Western markets for export revenues and on Asian partners for imports , shaping its economic and strategic calculus in the Indo-Pacific . Tables 1 , 2 , and 3 also highlight its need for functional bilateral partnerships for development and trade . <p> The need to strengthen these bilateral ties has increased in recent years . Economists opine that due to the impact of faulty policies , aggravated by the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russia -- Ukraine war , " the somewhat comfortable macroeconomic situation that Bangladesh -- with high economic growth , low inflation , and good foreign exchange reserves -- was experiencing for the last few years has now disappeared . " 31 This has resulted in rising inflation , declining foreign exchange reserves , and low remittance inflows. 32 Therefore , Dhaka 's dependence on partner countries has increased , as foreign funding could bail it out of an economic crisis . Accordingly , the former Awami League government pursued a cautious foreign policy ; given their distinct approaches to the geopolitics of the Indo-Pacific and China 's rise in the region , Dhaka 's ability to maintain ties with each country became a test of its diplomatic skills . Its 2023 IPO reflected its priority of strengthening ties with all its partner countries while retaining ' balance ' in its diplomacy . <h> A Neutrally Worded Document <p> While Bangladesh is a member of China 's BRI , it did not subscribe to the US Indo-Pacific Strategy , despite Washington 's request and its reliance on American markets for its RMG products , f because the Strategy seemed to have an anti-China orientation and might have strained Dhaka 's ties with Beijing. 33 Consequently , the US became apprehensive about China 's influence and started intervening in Bangladesh 's domestic politics , with frequent critiques of its handling of human rights issues and electoral irregularities. 34 Dhaka chose a middle path by embracing the Indo-Pacific concept but articulating this stance neutrally , thus soothing the US and avoiding Chinese displeasure . Accordingly , Washington noted a " significant overlap " between Bangladesh 's IPO and its own Indo-Pacific Strategy , " including on issues such as freedom of navigation and overflight ; open , transparent , and rules-based multilateral systems ; and environmental resilience. " 35 Many of the Quad 's areas of cooperation , including disaster risk reduction and health security , were prioritised in the IPO , without any overt reference to the grouping. g , 36 However , the IPO advocated a " rule-based multilateral system " to enable equitable and sustainable development in the Indo-Pacific , rather than the Quad 's preferred " rule-based order . " 37 <p> The IPO carefully avoided provoking China by asserting , " We are not following anyone . Our IPO is independent . " 38 It propounded the guiding principle of " Friendship towards all , malice toward none " and used " inclusive " in its articulation of a shared Indo-Pacific future. 39 It remained non-committal by not prescribing any measures to achieve its stated objectives . While some critiqued the IPO as a reflection of Bangladesh 's lack of an underlying plan , 40 this term lent it a more flexible connotation than a plan or strategy , retaining the necessary diplomatic ambiguity. 41 <h> Emphasis on Peace and Stability <p> Rather than refer to defence collaborations or military pacts , the IPO upheld international rules and conventions , particularly those given in the UN Charter. 42 One of its guiding principles was drawn from the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea ( UNCLOS ) : to strengthen " existing mechanisms on maritime safety and security in the Indo-Pacific " and uphold " the exercise of freedom of navigation &amp; over-flight. " 43 Bangladesh worked towards cooperation with all its Indo-Pacific partner countries to address maritime emergencies and conduct search-and-rescue operations , thus refraining from taking any geopolitical side , and focused on universally accepted security norms . It also promoted Track 2 diplomatic processes , such as strengthening mutual trust and respect through partnerships , cooperation , and dialogue . It emphasised a ' culture of peace , ' a UN declaration that Bangladesh played a key role in drafting in 1997. 44 <h> Silent on State-Centric Security Challenges <p> In line with its non-alignment policy , Bangladesh emphasised " non-interference in internal affairs " of other countries as a foundational principle. 45 Instead , it focused on human security challenges and global well-being . It highlighted humanitarian issues necessitating collective action , such as climate change , disaster risk reduction , biodiversity loss , marine pollution , food and health security , energy sustainability , and water cooperation . It advocated for women-led development , international non-proliferation , peacekeeping , peacebuilding , combating transnational organised crime , and counterterrorism . This underscored both Dhaka 's vulnerabilities and its substantial contributions to the UN 's peacekeeping missions. 46 Collaborating in these spheres with Indo-Pacific countries offered a triple advantage -- facilitating collective dispute resolution , strengthening partnerships , and upholding Bangladesh 's pivotal role in tackling human security challenges while championing global peace initiatives. 47 <p> These features of the IPO illustrate the essence of the ' Diplomacy of Balance . ' It shows that the IPO was neither against China nor aligned with the US ; it reflected Dhaka 's self-awareness of its place within the Indo-Pacific. 48 Sheikh Hasina 's tenure was , therefore , marked not only by lucrative partnerships but by instances where Bangladesh exercised restraint and even asserted its sovereign decision-making authority . <p> However , after the regime change in August 2024 , this approach , as well as the IPO , was set aside . While there was no news of the IPO 's termination or revision , it was withdrawn from the public domain , indicating that it did not align with the interim government 's priorities , given the latter 's noticeable attempts to break free from the ' Awami mould . ' 49 Under Chief Advisor Yunus , Bangladesh 's foreign policy took a clear break from the earlier established trajectories . This shift needs to be analysed to understand its impact on Bangladesh 's prospects and its future role in the Indo-Pacific region . <h> Changes in Foreign Partnerships <p> In June -- July 2024 , student protests , initially against the reservation of jobs for descendants of ' Muktijoddhas , ' h erupted across Bangladesh , which turned anti-government after a violent state crackdown. 50 The public discontent with the Awami League was escalated by political parties and groups to capitalise on the situation . Upon coming to power , the interim government began distancing itself from the Awami League 's legacy and affiliations to secure popular support. i , 51 This was reflected in its foreign policy as well . <h> The US -- From Cooling Ties to ' Strategic Indulgence ' <p> For most of Sheikh Hasina 's 15-year-long tenure , Bangladesh maintained strong ties with the US due to converging national interests. j This was reflected in the booming trade and development partnership . However , in the final years of her regime , Dhaka 's growing proximity to Beijing created friction with Washington. 52 In December 2021 , the US imposed sanctions on Bangladesh 's Rapid Action Battalion over allegations of human rights abuse. 53 In 2022 , the American ambassador to Bangladesh , Peter Haas , critiqued its human rights situation , doubting the possibility of conducting democratic elections in a " politically violent environment . " 54 In February 2023 , the US State Department Counsellor , Derek Chollet , warned that the decline of democracy in Bangladesh would limit cooperation with the US. 55 Bangladesh was not invited to the two Democracy Summits organised by the US in 2023 and 2021 , 56 and visa restrictions were imposed on any Bangladeshi believed to be undermining the 2024 election through actions such as vote rigging , voter intimidation , using violence to prevent people from exercising their right to free association and assembly , and attempts to prevent political actors ( parties and voters ) from freely expressing their views. 57 <p> While Hasina initially tried to assuage the US , continuing censure led her to chastise it for promoting a regime change by supporting opposition parties. 58 , 59 After her removal , news reports suggested a foreign hand at play , linked to an undelivered speech in which Hasina mentioned the US ' demand to hand over control of Bangladesh 's St. Martin 's Island to it , to have " sway over the Bay of Bengal. " 60 , 61 However , the US denied these claims . The Jamaat-e-Islami ( JeI ) , k Bangladesh 's largest Islamic political party that was banned by the Awami League , is believed to have leveraged the US ' increasing interest in Bangladesh to return to politics. 62 , 63 These developments indicated that the precarious ' Diplomacy of Balance ' had faltered . <p> Chief Advisor Yunus is reported to have had close ties with the US Democratic Party , especially the Clinton and Biden administrations. 64 His first international trip in September 2024 to attend the 79th session of the United Nations ( UN ) General Assembly also included a visit to the US to meet President Joe Biden. 65 However , this partnership was short-lived after the US regime change . Under the second Trump presidency , cuts to USAID-backed initiatives stopped several development projects in Bangladesh and reduced ODA to the country . This affected its economy , which was already encumbered by inflation and unemployment . <p> To make matters worse , in April 2025 , the Trump administration levied a 37 percent tariff on Bangladesh under the Reciprocal Trade Act , later reduced to 35 percent after negotiations , but still more than double the original 15.5 percent . This hit the RMG industry hardest -- it constitutes about 80 percent of Bangladesh 's exports , employs nearly 4 million people , and contributes roughly 10 percent of GDP . The tariff increased the risks of slower growth , job losses -- especially for women , who form the majority of the RMG labour force -- and a rise in poverty. 66 While the tariff was further reduced to 20 percent in August 2025 after successful negotiations , 67 RMG exports to the US fell by nearly 11 percent year-on-year in October 2025. 68 <p> Unlike the final years of the Hasina regime , the Yunus government refrained from harsh rebuttals , instead choosing a policy of compliance and negotiation to pursue its interests with the Trump government. 69 In his letter to President Trump , Yunus stated , " Bangladesh will take all necessary actions to fully support your trade agenda . " 70 This strategy led to a reduction in the tariff rate to 19 percent in February 2026 , and exemptions for certain textiles and garments produced with US materials under a bilateral trade agreement , giving Bangladesh 's apparel industry a more competitive position than other garment exporters such as Vietnam and India . However , analysts argue that the terms on which this was agreed raise questions about how much the trade deal serves Bangladesh 's national interests . For example , Dhaka agreed to provide preferential market access for US industrial and agricultural goods , potentially exposing its domestic agricultural and industrial products to competition and reducing government revenue from tariffs. 71 <p> Bangladesh also agreed to ease non-tariff barriers by accepting US vehicle safety and emissions standards , as well as US Food and Drug Administration certifications for imported products , and removing import restrictions on remanufactured goods . According to a news report , " Controversial genetically modified products can not be restricted under this deal , and Bangladesh can not even require mandatory labelling , which may pose a threat to public health . " 72 <p> Bangladesh also agreed to several purchases , including aircraft procurement , around US$3.5 billion worth of US agricultural products , and an estimated US$15 billion of US energy products , over 15 years . These deals will prevent it from importing these products from other nations at more competitive prices and faster delivery times , raising both financial costs and geopolitical risks. 73 <p> Bangladesh is the only country in South Asia to have concluded such a deal with the US , and its timing and nature suggest that the interim government prioritised international validation over national interest . This allegation is reinforced by the deal being concluded in secrecy days before the 13th general election in Bangladesh . There are more instances of the interim government favouring the US : in January 2026 , it expressed an interest in contributing troops to join a US-backed International Stabilisation Force in the Gaza Strip . Although this was part of a broader UN-authorised mission , Bangladesh 's offer is seen as a " strategic indulgence " of the Trump administration before signing the trade deal and amidst its visa restrictions . l , 74 <p> Indeed , Trump 's hard stance on immigration and restrictive visa policies , targeting Muslim-majority nations , increased anxieties among Bangladeshi immigrants in the US. 75 From January 2026 , Washington requires Bangladeshi nationals/citizens seeking B1 or B2 visas to pay a bond of US$5,000 , US$10,000 , or US$15,00076 -- refundable if the authorities record the applicant 's departure before the visa 's expiry , or if the applicant is unable to visit , or is denied entry . This amount would be out of reach for most Bangladeshi nationals , given that the country 's per capita annual income is estimated at US$2593.4 , 77 slightly more than half the amount required to pay the lowest bond . Bangladesh National Security Adviser Khalilur Rahman requested US Under-Secretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker to exempt Bangladeshi business persons from this ; however , the matter remains under consideration. 78 <p> Reports suggest that the US also seeks to build a port in Bangladesh as part of the Quad Ports of the Future Partnership. 79 While the Quad 's interests are at the forefront , this also indicates Washington 's desire for a firmer foothold in the Bay of Bengal , which is fast becoming a zone of power competition . A US port in this location would increase strategic competition in the Bay of Bengal region , not only with China , but also with India and Japan , which have already invested in this sector . <p> The BNP government will have to contend not only with responding to the demands of the Trump administration but with Beijing 's response to an increased US presence in Chattogram , where China has considerable investments . <h> China -- From a Balanced Engagement to an Overt Pivot <p> For China , Bangladesh , with its developing economy and burgeoning youth population , has economic and strategic potential . Its location provides maritime access to China 's landlocked western provinces , which can help it " break out of the East Asia mould and become a more global power . " 80 It allows Beijing a greater presence to keep a closer watch on the nearby Strait of Malacca , thus assuaging its ' Malacca Dilemma . ' m , 81 It is crucial to China for implementing the Maritime Silk Road under the BRI , which seeks to develop infrastructure projects in key littoral states along the great trade arteries in the Indian Ocean. 82 Thus , Beijing 's strategic interests converged with the former Awami League government 's desire for more foreign partnerships to boost infrastructural development , leading to a substantial increase in Chinese trade and investment . In 2006 , China surpassed India to become Bangladesh 's largest trading partner. 83 It constructed key infrastructure across the country , 84 invested heavily in the power sector , 85 and became its largest arms supplier. 86 <p> However , Hasina was " careful " about the development partnership with China amid global concerns over mounting debts to Beijing. 87 For example , in 2021 , after Beijing supplied emergency COVID-19 vaccines to Dhaka , the Chinese ambassador to Bangladesh warned that bilateral ties would be damaged if the latter joined the Quad. 88 Even though Bangladesh was desperate for vaccines , it demonstrated diplomatic skill by acknowledging China 's help while firmly asserting its autonomy to make independent choices. 89 Consequently , Chinese President Xi Jinping reassured Hasina of Chinese support in withstanding US pressure. 90 <p> However , the interim government displayed overt prioritisation of China . Yunus chose Beijing for his first bilateral official visit , 91 breaking Hasina 's tradition of visiting India first after electoral victories . This visit secured Bangladesh US$2.1 billion worth of investments and grants from China , n , 92 bringing the total Chinese investment to nearly US$42 billion in FY 2024 -- 25. 93 Yunus secured nine agreements for enhancing economic and technical cooperation , covering sectors from development projects , cultural exchanges , to the translation and publication of classical literary works . He urged China to lower interest rates on loans to Bangladesh from 3 percent to 1 -- 2 percent and requested a waiver of commitment fees on Chinese-funded projects in the country . He also expressed interest in working with China to develop the Chittagong China Economic and Industrial Park , reinforcing economic cooperation between the two nations . He proposed Chinese involvement in the modernisation and expansion of Mongla Port as well. 94 <p> However , several of these requests raised concerns about India 's strategic interests ; for instance , China providing a 50-year master plan for Bangladesh 's river management . It was particularly concerning in light of China 's plans to build a massive hydroelectric dam on the Yarlung Zangbo River in Tibet and could create serious environmental and security concerns for India and Bangladesh. 95 <p> Yunus also welcomed Chinese participation in the Teesta River Comprehensive Management and Restoration Project ( TRCMRP ) . 96 Sharing the Teesta River 's water has been the longest-standing issue between India and Bangladesh , one which both countries had earlier decided to resolve bilaterally . Hasina had refused China 's offer and instead accepted India 's proposal of executing a US$1 billion river development project on the Teesta . Her decision upheld the sanctity of Bangladesh 's bilateral ties and choices , as well as being considerate of New Delhi 's strategic sensitivities. 97 The interim government 's decision showcased its tilt towards China and strain with India . <p> This was further strengthened by Yunus 's controversial statement on India 's Northeast during his state visit to Beijing , where he remarked , " The seven states of eastern India , known as the Seven Sisters , are a landlocked region . They have no direct access to the ocean . We are the only guardians of the ocean for this entire region . This opens up a huge opportunity . It could become an extension of the Chinese economy -- build things , produce things , market things , bring goods to China and export them to the rest of the world . " 98 <p> Yunus also sought to foster greater cooperation with China in the healthcare sector , shifting it away from India . In August 2025 , a delegation comprising Bangladeshi patients , doctors , and travel agencies visited Kunming in China 's Yunnan province to explore medical treatment options . China also dedicated four hospitals in Kunming for Bangladeshi patients . Chinese authorities are considering operating direct flights from Chittagong to Kunming to make medical travel more feasible for Bangladeshis. 99 <p> Under the interim government , China emerged as the preferred bilateral partner . This is reflected in the 25 percent increase in Bangladesh 's imports of Chinese goods ( US$1.54 -- 1.92 billion ) and its 44.1 percent rise in exports to China ( US$90.4 -- 130 million ) between August 2024 and August 2025 , the period of the regime change , during which its trade with India faltered. 100 Beyond trade and investment , Bangladesh continued to receive Chinese support on the Rohingya issue . Soon after Yunus 's China visit , Myanmar declared that nearly 180,000 Rohingya refugees living in Bangladesh 's Cox Bazar were eligible to return . Beijing 's links with the authorities and the ethnically armed organisations in Myanmar increased its chances of negotiating a lasting solution to the Rohingya problem , making it a more promising partner for Bangladesh. 101 <p> However , while China responded with alacrity to Yunus 's diplomatic outreach , 102 it also reached out to other power centres in Bangladesh , most prominently the JeI , which is reported to be " anti-India " , " pro-Pakistan , " and has reportedly never criticised China for its treatment of Uyghurs. 103 , 104 , 105 In September 2024 , the Chinese ambassador to Bangladesh , Yao Wen , met with the JeI 's chief , Shafiqur Rahman , the first visit by a foreign diplomat to the party 's Dhaka office since 2010 . Subsequently , there have been more exchange visits between China and the JeI . The growing affinity between China and the JeI led to its popularity among a large section of Bangladesh 's youth , particularly the Islami Chhatra Shibir , the JeI 's student wing , which had won student elections at the country 's important academic institutions . Coupled with anti-India sentiments fanned by opposition to the former Awami League government , this explained the massive demonstrations at Chittagong University in October 2025 , which pressured the interim government to ensure faster implementation of China 's Teesta Project , even at the cost of India 's sensitivities. 106 <p> For the interim government , closer ties with China meant greater international validation . But this also carries risks . The current regime must remain cautious of the conditions attached to Chinese financing and the broader concerns surrounding Beijing 's debt-trap diplomacy. o , 107An overt tilt towards China could invite US displeasure and heighten tensions with India , thereby undermining regional stability and complicating Bangladesh 's neighbourhood diplomacy . <h> India -- From the ' Golden Chapter ' to Strained Ties <p> The convergence in foreign policy outlooks between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and former Bangladesh PM Hasina ushered in the Shonali Adhyay or ' golden chapter ' in their bilateral relations. 108 Hasina inherited her father 's legacy of amity with India , which became one of the most striking features of her foreign policy. p Several roadblocks were resolved during her tenure , q and the longstanding concern over sharing the Teesta River 's water did not hinder the two countries from cooperating in other sectors. 109 Bangladesh under Hasina was considerate of India 's sensitivities , r and New Delhi was keen for her government to remain in power. 110 Both countries sought to leverage their shared geography and resources for mutual benefit . <p> Bangladesh shares the world 's fifth-largest border with the Indian states of West Bengal , Assam , Tripura , Mizoram , and Meghalaya. 111 The Northeast forms Bangladesh 's hinterland for its transit trade with Nepal and Bhutan , while Bangladesh provides it convenient maritime access. s Bangladesh serves as India 's land bridge to Southeast Asia , crucial for New Delhi 's Act East and Neighbourhood First policies. t The two countries also collaborated in energy and trade of necessities. 112 India remains the leading destination for Bangladeshi medical tourists. 113 Bangladesh 's ' zero tolerance ' stance against the insurgent groups causing disturbances in India 's Northeast from its territory particularly helped New Delhi stabilise the region . Before the regime change , the two countries were exploring further defence cooperation and negotiating a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. 114 <p> However , Hasina 's rapport with India led to the August 2024 protests having a distinct anti-India undertone . The interim government capitalised on this to secure legitimacy . Hasina 's continued shelter in India in the face of an extradition plea , the recurrence of attacks on Hindu minorities in Bangladesh , and the interim government 's repeated attempts to blame India for its internal instability , as well as to strengthen ties with China and Pakistan , further undermined the partnership. 115 Chief Advisor Yunus met Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif twice during his brief tenure , leading to diplomatic cooperation across sectors . Pakistan 's military described the two nations as " brotherly countries " after Yunus 's efforts. 116 <p> The agenda-driven reimagination of Bangladesh 's history after the regime change was even more worrying for India . New history books in Bangladesh erased Mujibur Rahman 's poems , speeches , and articles , instead elevating former Army Chief Ziaur Rahman 's role in issuing the first public proclamation of Bangladesh 's independence in 1971 . Images of Hasina were removed , while the 2024 protests that toppled her government were valorised. 117 India 's role in perpetuating the ' Muktijuddho ' was thus undermined , eroding a fundamental pillar of trust in the bilateral relationship . <p> Trade between India 's Northeast and Bangladesh also declined , with border closures , heightened scrutiny in customs clearance , and increased security surveillance hindering the smooth flow of goods and severely impacting border-dependent livelihoods. 118 Connectivity was also impaired , with public transport between the countries suspendedu and India-backed development projects stalled indefinitely. 119 Matters came to a head when Yunus made the controversial statement to China about India 's Northeast . In response , India 's Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs revoked Bangladesh 's transhipment facility to export goods to third countries via Indian ports , ascribing it to complaints from Indian exporters about logistical delays , rising costs , and congestion due to Bangladeshi cargo. 120 This affected Bangladesh 's exporters , as Dhaka depended on India 's transhipment facilities for much of its overseas trade. v , 121 <p> The retaliation , however , had more triggers than Yunus 's politically questionable move of using a third country as a bargaining chip in bilateral negotiations and inviting China to work on the Teesta project . The interim government had reportedly invited Chinese investment to revitalise the airbase at Lalmonirhat , situated close to the narrow Siliguri Corridor , which connects the politically sensitive Northeast to the rest of the country . Naturally , New Delhi is cautious about the region 's security , and Bangladesh 's offer to station Chinese fighter jets in its proximity carried serious security implications. 122 <p> Yunus 's statement showed disregard for India 's sensitivities and a dearth of understanding of Bangladesh 's geopolitical reality . While Bangladesh 's ports provide better access to India 's landlocked Northeast , the Northeast can still reach the sea via the Kolkata Port . India also owns operational rights to the Sittwe Port in Myanmar . Consequently , the assertion that Dhaka was the " guardian of the ocean " overstated Bangladesh 's role and overlooked the broader regional maritime geography . Notably , New Delhi did not revoke Dhaka 's transit trade rights through the Northeast . This had two diplomatic motivations : first , to make the interim government realise the Northeast 's value as a critical hinterland and transit territory ; and second , to showcase India 's commitment towards its bilateral ties with Nepal and Bhutan , which rely on Bangladesh 's port for overseas trade. 123 <p> While Chief Advisor Yunus and Indian Prime Minister Modi met on the sidelines of the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation 's ( BIMSTEC ) sixth summit to discuss current challenges and encourage cooperation , these intentions remained only on paper. 124 India subsequently launched the Shillong -- Silchar corridor , a 166.80 km greenfield high-speed corridor from Mawlyngkhung in Meghalaya to Panchgram in Assam , which , if connected with Myanmar via the ongoing bilateral Kaladan Multimodal Transit Transport Project ( KMMTTP ) , will allow New Delhi to circumvent Bangladesh and provide the Northeast maritime access via the Sittwe Port. 125 <h> Continued Development-Centric Engagement with Japan , but an Uncertain Future <p> Japan has been one of Bangladesh 's most important and trusted development partners over the last five decades . The former 's search for markets in South and Southeast Asia led it to Bangladesh . Since 1972 , Japan has supported Bangladesh through ODA , funding several development projects. 126 <p> During the Hasina years , Japan played an increasingly prominent role in developing Bangladesh 's connectivity infrastructure , giving Dhaka some bargaining power vis- ? -vis Beijing . In 2014 , Japanese PM Shinzo Abe , in partnership with the Awami League government , launched the Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt ( BIG-B ) initiative to facilitate industrial development along the Dhaka -- Chattogram -- Cox 's Bazar belt and beyond . The aim was to position Dhaka as a regional economic hub and provide Tokyo easy access to neighbouring country markets. 127 As part of this initiative , Japan began constructing the Matarbari deep-sea port , modelled on its Kashima and Niigata ports. 128 As Bangladesh 's first deep-sea port , Matarbari is expected to ease pressure on Chattogram Port129 and increase transit trade with Nepal and Bhutan . Japan also undertook solar and thermal energy projects , out of which the Matarbari coal-fired power plant is nearing completion. 130 <p> Japan 's concept of a ' Free and Open Indo-Pacific ( FOIP ) ' emphasises trade liberalisation and expansion of economic opportunities in South Asia . Given that nearly 80 percent of Japan 's maritime trade passes through the Strait of Malacca , Japanese Ambassador to Bangladesh Ito Naoki highlighted the importance of cooperation for a peaceful , prosperous , and stable FOIP. 131 The vision emphasised integrating the development of Northeast India and Bangladesh as part of a broader Bay of Bengal community. 132 As a trusted partner of India already operating in the Northeast region , Tokyo 's projects in Bangladesh proved complementary under the Hasina governance . <p> Bangladesh 's importance to Japan is reflected in its choice of Dhaka as one of the four nations to receive the Official Security Assistance , a defence aid from Japan to select nations to ascertain the respective region 's " comprehensive defence architecture . " 133 Bangladesh -- Japan ties were further strengthened during Hasina 's last visit to Tokyo in April 2023 , when the two countries formed a security partnership , deciding to continue goodwill visits by the respective defence forces and establish defence and national security wings in their respective embassies . Bangladesh was also interested in defence technology transfers from Japan. 134 A joint study group was appointed to analyse the possibility of an Economic Partnership Agreement , 135 which was subsequently signed on 6 February 2026 . <p> The ties between the two countries have been essentially development-oriented , and Japan has never intervened in Dhaka 's home affairs. 136 It maintains its influence through economic diplomacy , development aid , and strategic partnerships , focusing on stability and economic growth rather than political engineering . Therefore , the ties between the two countries were unaffected by the regime change in Bangladesh . <p> Chief Advisor Yunus was well received during his four-day visit in May 2025 , when he met with Japanese Prime Minister Ishiba and signed Memorandums of Understanding ( MoUs ) on economic cooperation and investment , skill development of the Bangladeshi workforce , and employment in Japan . Yunus was able to secure budgetary assistance of US$1.063 billion , comprising a development policy loan for economic reform and climate change resilience worth US$418 million , a loan for a railway project worth US$641 million , and US$4.2 million in grants for educational scholarships. 137 The duty-free access that Bangladesh enjoyed in Japan 's market is coming to an end in 2026 with its graduation from LDC to developing nation . Bangladesh would have to pay export duties up to 10 percent on commodities shipped to Japan . To address this , the countries discussed signing an Economic Partnership Agreement ( EPA ) to grant duty-free access to Bangladeshi goods , which is now concluded. 138 <p> However , the growing political unrest in Bangladesh under the interim government became a cause of concern for Japan as it hampered the latter 's business prospects . Accordingly , JICA undertook risk assessments for development outcomes . Under the Awami League , Japanese investments advanced with a composed regularity , but during the interim government 's rule , Tokyo 's approach was more risk sensitive . Had domestic unrest persisted , Japan 's investments in Bangladesh would have become uncertain . <p> The shift from Hasina to Yunus marked not just a change in government , but a broader reorientation in Bangladesh 's external engagements . Under Hasina , Dhaka maintained a careful balance among its partners , cultivating strong ties with the US , China , India , and Japan while avoiding overt alignment . Under Yunus , this calibrated approach gave way to a more uneven pattern : ties with the US were restored , but often on asymmetrical and indulgent terms ; China became a more preferred partner ; engagement with India deteriorated ; and ties with Japan remained development-centric but subject to concerns over domestic instability . <p> Despite these shifts , Bangladesh 's long-term economic prospects remain linked to continued development investments , trade access , infrastructure financing , and strategic partnerships with all four countries . It is therefore necessary to explore the implications of these shifts in Bangladesh 's foreign policy for its prospects in the Indo-Pacific . <h> Implications of Foreign Policy Shifts <p> By design , an interim or " caretaker " government exercises limited authority , as it is mandated primarily to oversee elections and ensure a smooth transition to an elected administration . Therefore , the frequency of the foreign visits undertaken by the unelected head of the interim government in Bangladesh has raised questions about their legitimacy . While some saw these trips as efforts to secure international recognition for the transitional regime , others viewed them as attempts to shape Dhaka 's strategic realignments. 139 <p> In 2025 , Yunus undertook an unusually active programme of foreign travel . Media reports indicated that he had made 11 -- 12 international visits within 10 -- 12 months , including to the UK , the US , the United Arab Emirates ( UAE ) , China , and Japan . Most of these visits were on the sidelines of international and multilateral engagements. 140 <p> These concerns about the interim government 's right to shape foreign policy were compounded by the contested nature of the caretaker government system itself . In 2011 , the arrangement was abolished through a Constitutional Amendment Act . Although the High Court Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court " partially annulled the Fifteenth Amendment to the Constitution and reinstated the non-partisan , neutral caretaker government system , " thereby legalising the Yunus administration , it remained an unelected government . Consequently , debates persisted over the limits of its authority and if its foreign policy initiatives reflected the preferences and mandate of the Bangladeshi populace. 141 Whether Bangladesh 's changing role in the Indo-Pacific was an engineered shift to suit sectional ambitions or it truly mirrored the people 's aspirations became a matter of debate . Nonetheless , the interim government 's policies marked a shift in Bangladesh 's important foreign partnerships , a foundation on which the elected BNP government would have to build its future policy in the Indo-Pacific and which would affect the country 's trade and development prospects . <p> Hasina 's ' Diplomacy of Balance ' was replaced by Yunus 's concept of " reaching out to everybody . " 142 While this justified attempts to diversify partnerships , including Dhaka 's engagement with Pakistan , it did not explain the deterioration of ties with New Delhi . It is in relation to India that the interim government 's foreign policy diverged most from the Awami League , apparently without due consideration of the organic dependencies between the two countries and Bangladesh 's national interests . <p> India and Bangladesh share not only history , culture , language , religion , people , and heritage , but also contiguous territories , 54 transboundary rivers , and adjacent maritime zones . This organic interdependence makes any imposed restraint unlikely to be economically or socially feasible . For example , in 2024 , the interim government retained a ban on exporting Hilsa fish to India during the festival of Durga Puja , in a break from the Awami League 's traditional Hilsa diplomacy , citing insufficient stock left for the domestic populace . However , this was a populist move to dissociate itself from the Awami League . Illegal trade and cross-border smuggling soon flourished , with Bangladesh 's local fish sellers selling at almost double and triple the price . Subsequently , the ban had to be lifted following rising " appeals by exporters . " The Yunus government was compelled to permit 3,000 tons of this prized fish to cross the border. 143 <p> Similarly , the restrictions imposed on medical tourism affected people in both nations . For Bangladeshis , Kolkata is the most convenient destination for treatment , due to its health facilities and its linguistic and cultural commonalities . However , due to the political turmoil in Bangladesh , visas were restricted for emergency and humanitarian needs only . Patients were unable to bring attendants along ; some even missed doctors ' appointments or surgeries . When visa operations were resumed after the regime change , they were substantially scaled down , sparking protests outside India 's visa application centre in Dhaka on 26 August 2024. 144 <p> India 's Union Budget 2026 -- 27 reduced financial assistance to Dhaka by 50 percent , from INR 120 crore to INR 60 crore . This aligns with a broader trend of slower project utilisation and India 's concerns regarding its bilateral ties and minority protection in Bangladesh. 145 Strained ties between Bangladesh and India are not empirically tenable for either country . Neighbours benefit when their aspirations and apprehensions align . <p> Weakened ties with New Delhi had even more implications . Under Sheikh Hasina , strong bilateral ties with India provided Bangladesh with a credible alternative to balance Beijing , to an extent . Under the interim government , China 's influence and investments in the country rose palpably , at the cost of India 's strategic interests . This exposed Dhaka to overdependence on China and the possible pitfalls of its ' debt-trap ' diplomacy . Furthermore , with increased Chinese presence in Bangladesh , the possibilities of friction with India increased , especially along sensitive border points . <p> An increased Chinese presence in Bangladesh is also a possible reason for the disenchantment of its other Indo-Pacific partner countries , such as Japan and the US . During the Hasina years , close ties with India , robust economic engagement with China , sustained development cooperation with Japan , and access to the US market together created a degree of balance . Under the interim government , this equilibrium weakened considerably . As Chinese influence and investments rose , especially in strategically sensitive sectors such as ports , river management , and infrastructure near border areas , Bangladesh risked being perceived less as a balanced regional actor and more as a site of Great Power competition . Such perceptions had the potential to reduce Dhaka 's diplomatic flexibility and lead to strategic vulnerability . <p> For Japan , this development could complicate the logic of its long-term engagement with Bangladesh . Japanese-backed projects in Bangladesh have been built on the assumption that the country would remain politically stable , economically viable , and strategically open to multiple partners . A pronounced tilt towards China , particularly if accompanied by domestic instability and strained ties with India , might compel Japan to reassess its future commitments . Japan -- China relations have been tense in 2025 -- 26 , marking one of their lowest points in years . However , Tokyo is unlikely to withdraw from Bangladesh abruptly , given the scale of its investments and Dhaka 's importance to its regional connectivity plans . <p> The US under President Trump is also likely to respond unfavourably if Bangladesh continues to align with China . Unlike the Biden administration , which foregrounded democracy and human rights , Trump 's approach appears more transactional , with trade access , market concessions , and strategic positioning taking precedence . In such a framework , Bangladesh 's value lies not only in its export potential but also its location in the Bay of Bengal . If Dhaka is seen facilitating an expanded Chinese strategic footprint while simultaneously seeking concessions from Washington , the US may tighten trade terms , reduce assistance , or extract further commitments . The interim government 's concessions to the US , discussed earlier , suggest that Dhaka 's room for autonomous bargaining may already be narrowing . In fact , two days before the 2026 elections in Dhaka , US Ambassador to Dhaka Brent T. Christensen stated , " The United States is concerned about growing Chinese influence in South Asia and is committed to working closely with the Bangladeshi government to clearly communicate the risks of certain types of engagement with China " and that President Trump would " like to see a good relationship between Bangladesh and India to support stability in the region . " 146 <p> Bangladesh 's future in the Indo-Pacific will depend on its ability to prevent external partnerships from becoming mutually antagonistic . The region represents a wide strategic environment for Bangladesh , within which its development , trade , connectivity , and security are embedded . A foreign policy that privileges one power at the expense of others might bring short-term gains but risks reducing Dhaka 's strategic autonomy , unsettling its neighbourhood ties , and undermining the diversified partnerships on which its economic future depends . <h> Conclusion <p> For the newly elected BNP government , the challenge is not just to inherit the foreign partnerships shaped by the interim regime , but to recalibrate them in a manner that restores credibility , balance , and national interest to Bangladesh 's external engagement . This will require rebuilding trust with India , preserving development-centric ties with Japan , managing economic relations with China without slipping into overdependence , and engaging the US without conceding disproportionate strategic or economic ground . Bangladesh 's long-term prospects in the Indo-Pacific will depend on its ability to pursue a calibrated diplomacy that sustains development while avoiding entanglement in great power contestation . <p> The banning of the Awami League from Bangladesh 's political scene has heavy implications for Bangladesh 's future , as the established trajectories of its ' Diplomacy of Balance ' are unlikely to return . Despite its history of uneasy ties with India , the BNP is intent on cultivating the relationship afresh , as is New Delhi . India readily acceded to the new Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman 's request for diesel amid the ongoing fuel crisis in 2026 . The connectivity projects stalled during the interim government 's era have also been resumed . However , New Delhi understands that any " overt embrace " of the new BNP government could trigger a nationalist backlash in Bangladesh. 147 Sheikh Hasina 's continued shelter in India will remain a point of contention ; hence , the BNP administration and India should rekindle their ties slowly , carefully , and steadily . <p> The BNP has historically maintained good relations with China , dating back to the time of party founder President Ziaur Rehman . Hence , it is likely that Tarique Rehman will continue to work towards fostering close multi-sectoral relationships . However , the approach is likely to be more balanced than the interim government 's . This is because the BNP is more politically experienced and Beijing too continues to engage with various political powers within Bangladesh , necessitating the Tarique administration to forge multiple partnerships and reduce dependence on a single external ally . In March 2025 , a 22-member delegation of Bangladeshi political leaders , civil society activists , academics and journalists , including BNP members its allies , and representatives of the National Citizens Party , undertook a 10-day visit to China. 148 Clearly , China does not want to put all its eggs in one basket . <p> A balanced approach towards China would also help deepen Dhaka 's development partnership and trade with Japan . Therefore , the BNP 's engagement with Tokyo is likely to prosper . Japanese Ambassador to Dhaka Shinichi Saida asserted that the EPA with Bangladesh matched the BNP manifesto 's focus on economic growth . Terming the strategic partnership founded on trust and shared values , he hoped that the new administration would restore law and order and economic growth through enhanced investment. 149 This underscores the importance of stability within Bangladesh and in the region , such as that attained through partnerships with neighbouring countries like India , and will be central to ensuring a business-friendly environment for Japanese investments . <p> Regarding the US , the BNP may need to review the trade deal signed by the interim government which has been termed as " extremely discriminatory . " 150 However , it would have to be wary of the unpredictability of the Trump regime . This reinforces the need to cultivate a BNP version of Bangladesh 's ' Diplomacy of Balance , ' upholding the country 's autonomy to make independent choices , ensuring the sustainability of its strategic partnerships without compromising national interests , and thereby securing Dhaka 's future in the Indo-Pacific . <p> The BNP has inherited a complicated legacy . Yunus 's foreign policy was largely oriented towards external support and internal validation . In the process , it had become polarised , with the risk of Bangladesh becoming a contested strategic space , in which external actors would play a bigger role in shaping its economic choices , security environment , and diplomatic autonomy . The BNP 's strong mandate , however , lends it the authority to undertake initiatives in line with Bangladesh 's national interests . @@138563900 <h> 40 ? C and counting : Europe was built to beat the cold . Now heatwave is exposing its biggest weakness <p> For centuries , Europe knew how to fight the cold.Its homes were built to trap warmth . Thick walls , insulated roofs , double-glazed windows and tightly sealed buildings helped people survive long winters . Entire energy systems were designed around one question : how to keep people warm when temperatures fell below freezing.Now that old design logic is being tested by a new climate reality.As deadly heatwaves become more frequent across Europe , the continent is discovering that buildings meant to hold heat in winter can become dangerous heat traps in summer . The latest heatwave has exposed a vulnerability decades in the making : Europe was built for heating , but it is now struggling with cooling.The warning signs are no longer limited to weather charts . Roads have buckled , train services have been disrupted , schools have shut classrooms , power grids have come under strain and hospitals have reported a surge in heat-related cases . @@138564586 <h> Berlin 's use of water cannons to cool tourists during a 40 ? C heatwave has sparked global attention . Doctors explain the science behind water cooling , its benefits , limitations and how it helps reduce heat stress . <p> As Europe heatwave continues to go on , Berlin has found an unusual way to help people beat the heat : water cannons . Normally associated with riot control , Berlin police recently repurposed two water cannon trucks to spray fine arcs of water over tourists and residents gathered near landmarks including Brandenburg Gate , Potsdamer Platz and the Reichstag . The move came as temperatures in parts of Germany climbed above 40 ? C , prompting authorities to issue heat warnings and deploy emergency cooling measures . <p> The scenes quickly went viral . Smiling tourists stretched out their arms to catch the cooling mist , while others welcomed the unexpected relief from the relentless sun . But beyond the dramatic visuals lies an important health question : Can getting sprayed with water actually protect you from dangerous heat ? <h> What Doctors Have To Say <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ yes , with some important caveats . " The human body cools itself mainly by sweating , " explains Dr. Renee Salas , emergency physician and climate and health expert at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health . Sweat evaporates from the skin , carrying heat away from the body in a process known as evaporative cooling . When temperatures soar above normal body temperature , or when you 're producing heat through walking or standing in the sun , this natural cooling system can become overwhelmed . Adding water externally mimics this process . <p> Whether it 's a misting station , a spray bottle , a garden hose or , in Berlin 's case , a water cannon set to a gentle spray , water on the skin evaporates and removes heat from the body , helping lower skin temperature and reduce thermal strain . It 's not just about feeling cooler Dr. W. Larry Kenney , professor of physiology at Pennsylvania State University and one of the world 's leading heat stress researchers , has spent decades studying how the body responds to extreme temperatures . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reduces cardiovascular strain during heat exposure . In extreme heat , the heart works harder to pump blood toward the skin so heat can escape . If cooling methods reduce skin temperature , the heart does n't have to work as intensely . This can be especially important for older adults , whose bodies sweat less efficiently and struggle to regulate temperature . <p> Berlin Water Canon ( Credits : X ) <p> Doctors also point out that the cooling effect does n't come simply from getting wet . It 's the evaporation afterwards that does most of the work . In dry climates , water evaporates rapidly , producing almost immediate relief . In humid weather , however , evaporation slows down because the air is already saturated with moisture . That 's why someone can feel unbearably hot even after getting drenched if humidity levels are high . Germany 's heatwave has largely been characterised by hot , relatively dry air , making misting and water sprays particularly effective . <h> What WHO recommends <p> Health agencies around the world recommend using water as one of the simplest @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the World Health Organization and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention includes taking cool showers , wetting the skin with damp towels , using misting fans and applying cool water to exposed skin during heatwaves . <p> The principle remains the same regardless of whether the water comes from a shower , a spray bottle or a specially adapted water cannon . But water alone wo n't stop heatstroke Doctors caution that while water spraying provides genuine relief , it is not a substitute for proper heat protection . If someone is developing heat exhaustion or heatstroke , simply getting wet will not reverse the condition . <p> Heatstroke is a medical emergency in which core body temperature typically rises above 40 ? C , and symptoms can include confusion , dizziness , rapid heartbeat , fainting and altered consciousness . In such cases , rapid cooling , emergency medical attention and hydration become critical . Likewise , standing in direct sunlight after being sprayed may provide only temporary relief if the person continues to lose fluids through sweating . <p> Europe heatwave ( Credits : X ) @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Berlin is n't the only city experimenting with creative cooling strategies . Italy , France , Spain and Poland have also expanded public cooling infrastructure during recent heat emergencies . Urban health researchers increasingly view these interventions as part of " heat adaptation " -- small environmental changes that reduce heat exposure for thousands of people in public spaces . <p> So , do Berlin 's water cannons really work ? Doctors say yes . <p> A gentle spray of water can lower skin temperature , enhance evaporative cooling , reduce the strain on the heart and provide immediate comfort during extreme heat . @@138577534 <h> We Are Part of the Ecosystem , Not The Ecosystem Itself <p> We humans have long carried the tendency to place ourselves above everything we can perceive as weaker than us . As Hobbes observed , " Human beings are selfish by nature " . And even in the age of unprecedented global interdependence , this observation continues to resonate . While we have become more connected through multilateral trades , tech advancement and better communication , we have certainly become more disconnected from the very foundation that sustains our existence . <p> Today , the world appears increasingly uncertain . Climate change is accelerating , carbon emissions continue to rise , freshwater resources are under immense pressure , trust deficits are affecting economies . Additionally global trade , conflicts and humanitarian crises persist and environmental degradation is fracturing the entire existence of these sophisticated and human made rules and proceedings . Amid all this uncertainty , we rarely pause to ask ourselves a simple yet fundamental question : Where are we actually heading ? <p> Somewhere along this journey of economic progress and technological progress , we have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ its owner , controller or master . We often speak about " Saving nature " as though we stand outside it . But nature does n't need saving from itself , it needs relief from the pressures created by human activities . Long before we existed , the ecosystem evolved , adapted and flourished . They are capable of healing but not at the pace at which we continue to exploit them . <p> Ironically , overtime sustainability has become one of the most frequently used words in public policy discussions , corporate reports and international conferences . Yet , how often do we truly reflect what it actually means ? Sustainability is not simply about sustaining economic growth or maintaining our current lifestyle . It is about sustaining the natural systems that make life possible . Every product we consume , every Kilometer we travel and every resource we extract carries an ecological cost that is often invisible to us . <p> Have we not confused DEVELOPMENT AND GROWTH in between ? Of course , development is essential . Better healthcare , education , infrastructure , transportation and technology @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ one wishes to return to a world without these opportunities . The challenge , however , lies in confusion between the two . Growth measured only through production and consumption can not be called progress if it depletes forests , pollutes rivers and destabilizes the climate . True development is inclusive . It improves human well being while protecting the ecology upon which all the species are depended upon . <p> Perhaps , the greatest environmental crisis is not climate change itself but the belief that humans exist separately from nature . And before asking what governments , industries or international organizations should do , perhaps we should ask ourselves a more uncomfortable question : Do we truly understand the environmental cost of our own choices ? We are not separate from nature nor we are its masters . We are simply one species among millions , dependent on an intricate web of life that has sustained this planet for ages . The day we begin to see ourselves as participants in the ecosystem rather than rulers of it , sustainability will no longer be a slogan .
