@@138582888 <h> Published on Jun 30 , 2026 <h> Quick Notes <p> In the global energy policy discourse , demand-side management ( DSM ) has become synonymous with the renewable energy transition . In energy policy discussions on grid flexibility required to accommodate intermittent renewables , smart meters , time-of-day tariffs , and sophisticated digital platforms designed to shift consumption to match the ebb and flow of solar and wind generation are repeatedly mentioned . But long before ' demand response ' became a buzzword in the context of managing intermittency , India had developed one of the world 's most extensive and arguably one of the most sophisticated DSM systems , born not of environmental idealism but of sheer necessity . <p> For much of the post-independence period , India 's electricity sector was characterised by chronic supply deficits . Faced with demand persistently exceeding available generation , system operators confronted two options : ( i ) permit grid collapse or ( ii ) actively manage demand . India adopted the latter course , thereby becoming an inadvertent pioneer in DSM . While technically rational from an engineering perspective , this approach disproportionately burdened rural consumers , exploiting pre-existing asymmetries of wealth and political voice between rural and urban populations . <p> The logic was brutally simple . Agricultural and rural household demand had a significant share in total demand for electricity , which was temporarily flexible . Farmers needed electricity to pump water for irrigation , but unlike industrial processes or urban residential lighting , pumping could often be shifted to off-peak hours without catastrophic consequences . Although rural households numerically exceeded their urban counterparts , and continue to do so , their share of electricity consumption remained markedly lower . More critically , rural households were neither mobilised nor sufficiently articulate in voicing grievances over power outages . This flexibility made agricultural and rural household electricity consumption ideal for load management . <p> The most straightforward intervention was load shedding itself . For example , in Maharashtra , a load-shedding protocol devised during the period of acute power shortages from roughly 2005 to 2012 systematically reduced supply hours to agriculture and rural households . Farmers and rural households received power on a rotating basis , eight hours during the day and ten hours at night in some formulations , while non-agricultural consumers received priority access . This was DSM in its most elemental form : the deliberate curtailment of consumption to prevent system collapse . <p> But India 's DSM innovations went far beyond simple load shedding . The most ambitious and consequential intervention was feeder segregation , pioneered by Gujarat under the Jyotigram Yojana ( Jyotigram Scheme ) launched in 2003 and substantially completed by 2006 . Prior to this initiative , rural villages typically received power through mixed feeders that served both agricultural pumps and domestic consumers on the same network . This created a fundamental problem . When the utility needed to manage demand , it had to cut power to entire villages , depriving households of lighting and other essential services . <p> The Jyotigram Yojana solved this by constructing separate 11 kV ( kilovolt ) feeders exclusively for agricultural pump sets . Physical feeder separation allowed the utility to manage agricultural demand independently of other rural consumption . Agriculture could receive power during off-peak night hours , when residential and commercial demand was low , while domestic consumers received reliable supply during peak periods . The scheme 's primary objective was to ' flatten the load curve with enough margins for morning peak and evening peak by arranging the time schedule of agricultural feeders round the clock ' . <p> The results were remarkable . In Gujarat , the maximum-to-minimum demand ratio improved dramatically , from 2100 MW/900 MW ( megawatt ) before implementation to 1850 MW/1450 MW afterwards . The load curve flattened throughout the day , reducing the strain on generation capacity and transmission infrastructure . Other states followed suit . Maharashtra implemented its own feeder separation scheme , carving out agricultural feeders from mixed networks and enabling the utility to stagger approximately 2500-3000 MW of demand . Despite the benefit of flattening the load curve , separation of feeders involved high capital costs , which prevented its nationwide adoption . <p> Maharashtra also pioneered another ingenious DSM measure , the single phasing scheme . The concept was elegantly simple . Agricultural pump sets require three-phase power to operate . By providing three-phase supply for only a limited number of hours each day and single-phase power for the remainder , the utility could effectively limit the hours during which pumps could run without cutting power entirely . This was DSM achieved not through sophisticated digital controls but through a basic understanding of electrical engineering and consumer behaviour . <p> By 2013 , Maharashtra had implemented single phasing in 15,000 villages and independent feeder separation in 18,000 villages . Together with capacity additions , these DSM measures helped reduce the state 's power deficit from 18 percent to just 3 percent over five years . The Forum of Regulators , India 's apex regulatory body , formally recognised agricultural DSM as a core strategy for reducing peak demand and shifting consumption to off-peak periods . <p> What makes this history remarkable is its prescience . Today , energy policymakers around the world are grappling with a challenge that India effectively solved , at least in part , decades ago : how to match electricity demand with variable supply . The challenge with renewables is that generation is intermittent ; solar output peaks during the day and falls to zero at night , while wind generation fluctuates with weather patterns . The solution , increasingly , is demand flexibility or shifting consumption to times when renewable generation is abundant . <p> By shifting agricultural pumping to night hours , Indian utilities were effectively matching demand to the availability of base-load thermal generation , which could run more efficiently at night when overall system demand was lower . The principle is identical to what modern DSM programmes seek to achieve with renewables , which is to align consumption with generation patterns to reduce the need for expensive storage or curtailment . This is not to suggest that India 's approach was perfect or that it can be directly replicated elsewhere . The political , economic , and institutional contexts are unique . But the underlying insight that large , flexible loads can be managed to match supply patterns is universal . <p> Recent research has begun to quantify the value of this approach . A study using agricultural load data from two distribution utilities in Gujarat estimated that agricultural load control already reduces total system costs by 5 percent , or approximately US$6.26/MWh ( megawatt hour ) of agricultural consumption . As India scales up its renewable energy capacity to reach the target of 500 GW ( gigawatt ) by 2030 , the agricultural sector 's role in providing demand-side flexibility is likely to become even more valuable . Agricultural pumping and space cooling remain the two largest contributors to peak demand , making agriculture an ideal candidate for demand response programmes that could absorb excess solar generation during the day . <p> India 's experience with agricultural DSM also offers important lessons about the limits of DSM . As many states subsidised electricity tariffs for agricultural consumers and for poor rural households , subsidised electricity also meant no electricity . This justified frequent supply outages imposed on agricultural and rural consumers . The result has been a system that manages demand through rationing rather than through price signals or efficiency incentives a crude but effective approach that has nevertheless perpetuated the underlying inefficiencies . <p> Reduction in supply hours to agriculture has real consequences for farmers and groundwater resources . When power is available for only a limited number of hours , farmers have an incentive to pump as much water as possible during those hours , potentially exacerbating groundwater depletion . The hours of supply to agriculture have declined in many states over the past decade , raising questions about the sustainability of this approach . <p> Today 's electricity retailers are , in effect , replicating the consumer segregation strategies that Indian grid managers adopted decades earlier . Historically , segregation was structurally imposed : rural consumers , constrained by limited purchasing power , were compelled to tolerate outages with minimal protest , whereas affluent and articulate urban consumers were offered minimum outages . Market mechanisms perform a similar function . The price metric will differentiate between consumers willing to accept lower tariffs in exchange for exposure to outages and those prepared to pay premium rates to secure uninterrupted supply . Ironically , this market-based stratification is likely to reproduce the very socio-economic divisions that earlier grid management practices had entrenched . <h> Monthly News Commentary : NON-FOSSIL FUELS <h> Nuclear Projects Gather Steam <h> India <p> Nuclear <p> NTPC Ltd has initiated site selection studies in four states , including Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh , to set up nuclear projects as part of its long-term 30 gigawatt ( GW ) nuclear energy plan . @@138587733 <h> Representative image . Photograph : ( Pexels ) <p> With a delayed southwest monsoon , 2026 is expected to deliver below-normal rains for India . India Meteorological Department ( IMD ) had earlier estimated rainfall at around 90 -- 92 per cent of the Long Period Average ( LPA ) . June has already signalled a weaker monsoon for the country , recording nearly 40 per cent below normal rains , making it one of the driest June in more than a decade and the fifth driest since India began keeping records in 1901 . This suggests the monsoon , which accounts for nearly 70 per cent of the country 's annual rainfall , is not just getting weak but also increasingly erratic in its behaviour . <h> A delayed start and uneven distribution <p> This year has seen a delayed onset and fragmented progression of weather systems that result in the monsoon . Arriving late over Kerala , the monsoon stalled in central and western India before showing intermittent revival , which resulted in long dry spells with short bursts of heavy rain . This pattern is becoming @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a Preferred Source <p> Meteorologists note that this " start-stop " behaviour is as significant as total rainfall deficits , because it disrupts soil moisture buildup and agricultural planning . <p> The southwest monsoon accounts for nearly 70 per cent of India 's annual rainfall . This seasonal rainfall supports the agriculture sector of the nation . According to government data , nearly 64 per cent of Indians rely on agriculture for their livelihood . Yet only around 55 per cent of the country 's net sown area is covered by irrigation infrastructure , leaving a large portion of farmland dependent on rainfall . This makes the success or failure of the monsoon a major factor in crop production . <h> Agriculture feels the early shock <p> The weak and uneven rainfall impacts India 's kharif sowing season . As per early estimates , there is a significant drop in acreage for major crops like rice , soybean , cotton , and maize . In some regions , soybean sowing has drastically fallen compared to last year , while rice cultivation has also slowed due to delayed rainfall . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ supported by irrigation , have shown relative stability . The early disruption of farming activities highlights how sensitive India 's agriculture remains to monsoon timing rather than just total rainfall . <h> Climate drivers behind the shift <p> According to the Indian Meteorological Department ( IMD ) , climate change is a driving factor leading to unpredictable or inconsistent monsoon rainfall . While some regions experience intense rainfall in short periods , others face prolonged dry spells . Climate change is also resulting in extreme weather events like heavy rainfall , floods , heatwaves and droughts . <p> The changing weather patterns across the world have also resulted in El Nino , which occurs when sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean become significantly warmer than normal , weakening trade winds and altering global atmospheric circulation . An intense El Ni ? o may weaken monsoons in India and affect crop production , and in turn , food prices . In the past , El Nino conditions have resulted in major droughts in India , including in 1982 , 1987 , 2002 , 2009 and 2015 . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ trends , the monsoon in India appears to be changing structurally . The distribution of seasonal rainfall is becoming more unequal , with fewer wet days and more intense rainfall episodes , even though the overall amount may not always decrease significantly . <p> Recent studies suggest a rise in variability of rainfall along with frequent alternations between dry spells and heavy downpours . This has also led to floods in urban areas in some regions as sudden heavy rainfall overwhelms drainage systems even during generally weak monsoon years . <p> Monsoon 2026 brings to light a developing reality : India 's monsoon is not only getting weaker or stronger , but it is also becoming less predictable , more erratic , and more influenced by the dynamics of climate change .
